## 5\. Discussion

The results of our three studies provide evidence for the usability and value of AI-based chatbots in buyer–supplier negotiations. More specifically, we build upon established research on different negotiation approaches in a human-to-human context (i.e. [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)) and illustrate distinct performance outcomes (economic as well as psychological and relational) in a human-to-machine setting. While the findings did not confirm the interaction effects in question (H1 and H2), they confirmed that a competitively prompted chatbot leads to a higher price discount for the buying organization across all studies and a quicker negotiation duration as compared to a chatbot employing a collaborative negotiation approach (Studies 1 and 2). Suppliers trust the collaborative negotiation approach of the chatbot more fully and show higher outcome satisfaction, as well as a stronger desire for future interaction (across all studies) with this approach.

First, we find a significant effect for price discounts in all three studies: the chatbot achieved higher price discounts when it employed a competitive negotiation approach, disregarding item type (non-critical or bottleneck). When comparing the results regarding price discount across all three studies, we find that the chatbot achieved substantial savings, coming very close to the prompted goal of 10 % in both student samples (Studies 1 and 2). However, significantly lower savings (see [Appendix E](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1): between 1,1 % and 5,5 %) were achieved when negotiating with experienced negotiators (Study 3). Our findings regarding price discount contradict the previous findings of [Purdy et al. (2000)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51), who found a positive relationship between price discount and a (perceived) collaborative negotiation approach in a human-to-human negotiation setting. The contradicting findings can be explained by the fact a collaborative negotiation approach is mostly used and effective in repeated purchases with the same party ( [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35)). While the negotiation task in our study was described as a contract renewal (i.e. repeated purchase), participants essentially negotiated with the supplier (i.e. Charlie) for the first time and hence the interaction could have been perceived as a one-time negotiation with low expectation of future dealings – thereby explaining the superior performance of a competitive negotiation approach according to [Krause et al. (2006)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35).

Second, we find a significant effect on payment terms in our study with practitioners (Study 3): better payment terms for the buyer were achieved when the chatbot employed a competitive negotiation approach. While undergraduate students may possess foundational knowledge of various contract items, they may not be able to effectively integrate and make tradeoffs between multiple contract terms during negotiations, thereby often prioritizing price. Also, unlike students, experienced practitioners often better understand the direct financial impact of changing payment terms and are often more experienced in conducting multi-attribute negotiations. This may account for the more significant effect on payment terms observed in our practitioner study (Study 3) as compared to our student studies (Studies 1 and 2). Especially, [supply chain](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/supply-chain-management)[finance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/finance) research has considered payment terms in conjunction with other contractual terms such as order quantity (see e.g. [Li et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib38)) which illustrates this multi-attribute nature of negotiations and hence the advantage of experience in negotiations.

Third, we find a significant effect on negotiation duration. When faced with a competitively prompted chatbot, students conducted shorter negotiations as compared to practitioners, who might be less likely to shy away from assertive negotiation counterparts. When analyzing the chat interactions, we found that practitioners are inclined to find creative ways to convince the chatbot that a price discount of 10 % and/or an extension [of payment terms](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/terms-and-conditions) may not be feasible by referring for instance to the tough economic environment (i.e. inflation). Students, on the other hand, settle more quickly when faced with a competitively prompted chatbot and seem to be more easily intimidated by it. We observe that our student samples more frequently came to an agreement when pushed by a competitively prompted chatbot as compared to practitioners (see [Table 4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl4) above). We therefore extent existing body of literature that has shown that negotiation experience matters in fostering negotiation performance (see e.g. [Lumineau and Henderson, 2012](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib40); [Moran and Ritov, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib47); [Thompson, 1990](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib59))

Fourth, in addition to the economic outcomes, psychological and relational outcomes were measured through existing scales. In all three studies, we find significant effects for negotiation approach. Respondents indicated higher trust, higher outcome satisfaction, and a stronger desire for future interaction when facing a collaboratively prompted chatbot (versus a competitively prompted chatbot). We can therefore contribute to existing research on B2B negotiations between human buyers and suppliers ( [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)) and highlight the fact that this also holds for interactions between a human and an AI-based chatbot. In our study with practitioners (Study 3), we further find significant effects for item type: when a bottleneck item was negotiated, regardless of the negotiation approach, respondents indicated higher trust (benevolence) as compared to interactions in which a non-critical item was negotiated (see [Table 5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl5)). We therefore extend findings of [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) on human-to-human negotiations for different quadrants of the KPM by illustrating the necessity to consider the item type (and hence the power position of the buyer) and the resulting effect on trust as a negotiation outcome.

Fifth, as the verbal interactions between the partitioners and Charlie might be most realistic, we also conducted language analysis using LIWC software and the data derived from Study 3. Text analysis using LIWC software indicated that more similar communication styles between practitioners and the chatbot were prevalent when the chatbot used a competitive negotiation approach, while an analysis of the word count showed no substantial differences in the numbers of words used between the four group conditions.

## 6\. Conclusion

With the advent of technology, firms are increasingly employing AI-based chatbots in their processes. While research in other fields, such as marketing or sales, has already highlighted evidence for their success and usage, chatbots are currently an under-researched topic in the field of PSM. By conducting three experiments with undergraduate students, as well as experienced buyer-supplier negotiation professionals, we provide initial insights into how the negotiations of the future might look like and what the important _outcome-influencing factors_, both structural and behavioral, might be in this regard. This section will elaborate on the academic and managerial implications and then provide the limitations and future research avenues.

### 6.1. Academic implications

We contribute to contemporary knowledge about buyer–supplier negotiations in multiple ways. First, while research on AI in the field of PSM is increasing (e.g. [Guida et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib24); [Spreitzenbarth et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib55)), to our knowledge, this is the first study to test various _outcome-influencing factors_ (structural and behavioral) in negotiations between AI-based chatbots (buyers) and humans (suppliers). By drawing on existing research on outcome-influencing factors, such as the _negotiation approach_ or the _power balance_ (operationalized as spend item) in a human-to-human negotiation setting (see [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl2)), we provide novel insights into a human-to-machine negotiation setting. We extend previous work by [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) and demonstrate that AI-based chatbots provide value in various negotiation settings.

Second, we use experiments. This method is nascent in supply chain management ( [Carter et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib11)) and PSM research ( [Eckerd, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib19)). With three experimental studies using a between-subjects design and both student and practitioner samples, we advance the understanding of the behavioral dimensions of buyer–supplier negotiations and provide pioneering insights into the future landscape of buyer–supplier negotiations. Our findings demonstrate that the experimental results are consistent between student and practitioner samples, confirming the validity of using student samples to test hypotheses, a practice supported in disciplines such as psychology and marketing. This implies that future PSM research could rely more heavily on the use of student samples to explore complex negotiation dynamics, thus broadening the scope and feasibility of experimental designs. This could promote incorporating more behavioral and experimental approaches into PSM research to further inform the development of nuanced theories that account for psychological and relational factors in buyer–supplier interactions. Additionally, our work can allow future PSM studies to explore the impacts of GAI in these negotiations, providing a framework for examining the constantly evolving nature of buyer–supplier engagements.

### 6.2. Managerial implications

We also contribute to practice, as our study provides initial insights into how GAI can be leveraged for efficient buyer–supplier negotiations and two main managerial implications for professionals can be drawn from it. First, our results provide evidence on the _outcome-influencing factors_ regarding an AI-based chatbot in buyer–supplier negotiations, such as negotiation approach and item type. Our overall results indicate that buying organizations, or, rather, Chief Procurement Officers (CPOs) wishing to implement a negotiation chatbot must make a trade-off: higher _economic outcomes_ for one's own organization versus higher trust, outcome satisfaction, and desire for future interaction on the part of the counterpart (supplier), depending on which negotiation approach the chatbot will employ.

Second, while generative AI chatbots demonstrate effectiveness in controlled settings, they are not yet suitable for autonomous buyer–supplier negotiations at scale. However, they can effectively support specific negotiation tasks, while purpose-built AI negotiation tools are better suited for full-scale implementation. Similar to research by [Dinnar et al. (2021)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib16) on the use of AI in teaching negotiations, we see the value of our negotiation interface based on ChatGPT for negotiation training purposes. The prompts feeding ChatGPT can easily be adapted, which makes it possible to quickly develop and tailor training cases to mimic specific negotiation needs and contexts. This also enables buyers to perform one or more trial runs to prepare for an upcoming complex negotiation. Thus, AI-powered negotiation chatbots provide companies with a cost-efficient and effective approach to training employees and preparing them for upcoming negotiations.

### 6.3. Limitations and further research

Our research has several limitations that offer opportunities for future study. The first concerns our sample composition. While we initially tested our manipulations and setting with students who had limited negotiation experience, our main study focused on practitioners that are experienced in buyer-supplier negotiations. While we believe that our practitioner sample is representative, we are aware of some weaknesses, such as (1) data collection being performed online and partially remotely, (2) the sample being of average size, and (3) the participants residing in multiple countries that met the WEIRD (Western, educated, industrial, rich, and democratic) criteria ( [Carter et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib11)). Future research could replicate Study 3 with a larger practitioner sample in a guided in-person setting and with non-WEIRD participants. In this way, cross-cultural comparisons can be conducted.

A second limitation concerns our manipulations. We thoroughly tested our manipulations and found significant effects in all three studies, as indicated above. While our study is intended to provide initial insights into the negotiations of the future, further improvements in the operationalization of our manipulations, as well as development of further manipulations (i.e., contextual factors, such as relational type or relational history), as shown in [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl2), could be valuable next steps. In addition, we acknowledge that negotiations are often longer than 15 min and not based on a one-time interaction. Future researchers could address these issues by conducting multi-round negotiations in which switching between negotiation approaches is possible. This is described as “strategic adaptability” by [Heunis et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib27). This would simulate real buyer-supplier negotiations as closely as possible.

The third limitation concerns the comparability of the results. Extant research has found that “communication media can have a significant impact on negotiations” ( [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51), p. 162). While human-to-machine interactions are increasing in popularity, it would have been ideal to also compare these results ( _economic outcomes_ and _psychological and relational outcomes_) with online chat interactions between two humans and thus contribute to the existing knowledge on negotiation medium ( [Croson, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib14); [Galin et al., 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib20); [Loewenstein et al., 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib39); [McGinn and Keros, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib44); [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)).

While our use of [large language models](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/large-language-model) (OpenAI's ChatGPT) as the backend system revealed certain limitations of these models, notably their tendency to concede when challenged, this characteristic illuminates a crucial research frontier. Though this behavior created valuable training opportunities for negotiation skills development, it also highlights the need to explore how various AI architectures maintain negotiation positions under pressure. Future research using alternative AI systems could not only test model resilience but also help define the characteristics needed for AI to become a truly effective negotiation partner. As (procurement) organizations continue to integrate AI into their operations, understanding these dynamics will be essential for successfully merging AI within PSM and negotiation practices.

## Appendix E. Summary of the experiment plan

| EXPERIMENT PLAN |
| --- |
| **Design and Procedure** |
| - ⁃<br>  **Setting:** Employing a 2 (negotiation approach: collaborative vs. competitive) × 2 (item type: non-critical vs. bottleneck) between-subject experiment.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Sample:**<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  Study 1 and study 2: undergraduate business students from a large Dutch public university participated and received course credit for attending the experiment conducted on desktop computers in the university lab.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  Study 3: incorporates practitioners that work within procurement or sales to ensure validity of our findings, to learn about how participants with negotiation experience might perform, and to understand their perception of the negotiation interaction with the chatbot. Moreover, Study 3 differs due to the (mostly) remote set-up of data collection as roughly two-thirds of respondents participated online (compared students being in the lab) whereas one-third participated in an in-class guided experiment as part of procurement workshops. No monetary incentive was given but the assurance that the study's results would be shared after completion.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Procedure:** All studies adhered to the same standardized procedure. Initially, participants were directed to a survey page, where they provided their informed consent. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions, received background information on the negotiation task and were subsequently directed to a chat interface, initiating the negotiation process. Participants assumed the role of suppliers negotiating with a buyer-company for contract renewal (straight-rebuy). The items under negotiation varied by condition: standardized office desks in the non-critical item condition and customized powerbanks in the bottleneck condition. The buyer is represented by an AI-based chatbot which we named “ProcureBot Charlie” with which participants negotiate via a web-based chat interface (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1) for an illustration). Participants were made aware that they were negotiating with a non-human counterpart in the introduction text of the study as well as by verbally (“ProcureBot”) and graphically illustrating Charlie as an AI-based chatbot (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). Charlie was based on OpenAI's GPT-3 model (Model: GPT-3.5-turbo), which is primed with background information and prompts for each of the four group conditions (see [Appendix B](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). In each of the four different conditions, ChatGPT was asked to reach a ten percent price discount and increase payment terms to ten days. All other contract items such as delivery terms or quantity were left open and could be flexibly addressed by both parties. For simplicity, key information of the negotiation assignment for each group was summarized on the chat interface (see also [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). Once the negotiation finished (maximum 15 min), participants were asked to end the negotiation and return to the survey page. In a second survey, participants were then asked to share their negotiation experience e.g. whether they reached agreement and if so, which terms were agreed upon (i.e. _economic outcomes_). Additionally, questions related to subjective perceptions (i.e. _psychological and relational outcomes_) about the outcomes were asked.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Quality Criteria:** same set of prespecified quality criteria across all studies. Participants with incomplete responses were excluded, as were those who failed the attention check. Additionally, negotiations that were too short to yield a meaningful outcome were excluded, with "too short" defined as negotiations that were 1.5 standard deviations below the mean negotiation length. [Table 3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl3) below provides an overview of our studies. |

## Highlights

- •
Analysis of the value of an AI-based chatbot in buyer-supplier negotiations.

- •
Three experiments: Participants take the role of the supplier, while a ChatGPT-based custom-trained chatbot acts as the buyer.

- •
A higher price discount, better payment terms and quicker negotiations are achieved by the chatbot when a competitive negotiation approach is taken.

- •
Suppliers trust a collaboratively prompted chatbot more, demonstrate a higher outcome satisfaction and desire for future interaction.


## Abstract

The technological breakthrough of artificial intelligence (AI) is impacting buyer-supplier negotiations, which are increasingly moving toward human-to-machine negotiations using AI-based chatbots. While the first AI-powered negotiation solutions are currently being used by procurement professionals to negotiate for non-critical spend items, which is an example of _structural influence_, the _behavioral influence_ of AI-based chatbots (i.e., on negotiation approach) remains unknown. It is unclear in which behavioral settings these chatbots deliver value to the buying firm in terms of economic, psychological, and relational outcomes. To fill this gap, we conduct three experiments in buyer–supplier negotiation settings, two in a lab-setting with undergraduate business students and one online experiment with professional negotiators. In our interactive simulations, participants play the role of the supplier, while a ChatGPT-based custom-trained chatbot acts as the buyer. We find that when the chatbot deploys a competitive, as compared to a collaborative, negotiation approach, it will achieve a higher [price discount](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/low-cost-strategy), better payment terms, and a quicker negotiation. However, suppliers trust a collaboratively prompted, as compared to a competitively prompted, chatbot more and demonstrate higher outcome satisfaction, as well as a stronger desire for future interaction. A text analysis of the chat interactions indicates a higher level of similarity when a competitively prompted chatbot is employed, which implies that suppliers also use more insistent and intimidating language, thereby matching the chatbot's negotiation approach to a greater degree. While the negotiation approach is a significant influencing factor, we do not find significant evidence that item type, in our case non-critical or bottleneck, matters, which indicates that AI-based chatbots can be effective in various buyer–supplier settings.

## 1\. Introduction

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) “has been emerging as a major force to trigger a truly enterprise-wide adoption of AI” ( [Kshetri et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib36), p. 1) with its ability to create new content, including text or images, by learning from patterns in existing data ( [Jackson et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib29)). The procurement function may possess a significant advantage regarding various GAI use cases, such as managing supplier performance or optimizing spend and demand. This is attributable to its strategic position at the intersection of vast amounts of data that are originating both internally and externally to the organization. It is predicted that especially for standardized spend items, value might be created, as buyers could leave the work to AI-based chatbots that can make purchasing decisions based on predefined objective criteria and instructions, thereby freeing up time for the buyers to focus on more strategic tasks ( [McKinsey, 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib45)). These chatbots, or conversational agents, “mimic interactions with real people by means of conversations through written and spoken natural language as well as gestures and other body expressions” ( [Mariani et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib42), p. 2) and are among the most widely used GAI tools in companies ( [Dencheva, 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib15)).

Interest in AI, including chatbots, has been increasing in the past few years in both academia and practice. The market for chatbots is estimated to grow by 22 % annually and projected to be worth 14 billion US dollars by 2025. The most common and well-known text-based chatbots are OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini. Consumer research, especially in marketing and sales, shows growing academic interest in chatbot applications ( [Mariani et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib42)). However, in the purchasing and supply management (PSM) domain, limited research on the applicability and usability of chatbots exists (B2B).

Reviewing the PSM literature on the use of AI, [Guida et al. (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib24) find that AI is especially useful in supplier selection and buyer–supplier negotiation processes. The authors highlight existing [industry](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/industry) applications, such as an AI-based negotiation coach that “can support the buyer in the preparation of conventional face-to-face negotiations and provide valuable insights for should-cost models used for auctions” (p. 2). Similarly, [Spreitzenbarth et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib55) highlight the potential usefulness of chatbots in supporting negotiations. Moreover, advanced automated human-to-machine negotiations are predicted to become especially useful for “smaller requisitions in the [long tail](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/niche-marketing-strategy) spend that have previously not been negotiated” (p. 13), as outlined by an industry expert. For example, chatbots are being increasingly used for buyer–supplier negotiations, as can be seen in the use of Pactum's technology at Walmart, the world's largest retailer. Walmart has achieved an average savings of 3 % on its tail-end spend through the implementation of an AI-based negotiation chatbot ( [van Hoek et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib61)).

Researchers have argued that chatbots can conduct creative and unique negotiation interactions that closely mimic human-to-human negotiation settings ( [Jackson et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib29)). However, it is unclear whether these automated negotiations using AI-based chatbots work in the same way as traditional human-to-human negotiations. Extant research has argued for the use of chatbots in negotiations over spend items belonging to a company's tail-end spend ( [Spreitzenbarth et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib55); [van Hoek et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib61)), which can be described as a _structural influence_, as it indicates the power dynamics and dependence within the buyer–supplier relationship ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33)). While _behavioral influence_, such as the approach chosen in negotiations, has been identified as particularly important in traditional human-to-human negotiations ( [McFarland et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib43)), the implications for human-to-machine negotiations remain unknown. It thus remains unclear which _negotiation approach_ on the part of the chatbot delivers the highest value to the buying firm and how a human seller (i.e., a supplier) will react to such negotiations. The extant literature on buyer–supplier negotiations identifies two main negotiation approaches: competitive and collaborative ( [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)). The former is characterized as aiming to achieve a one-sided goal by using threats and deception and being particularly successful in one-time purchases. The latter, on the other hand, aims at a mutually beneficial outcome for both parties; thereby, these parties may become interested in a repeated business interaction (e.g. [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)). In determining the suitable negotiation approach, the Kraljic Portfolio Matrix (KPM) provides distinct suggestions for various spend items ( [Kraljic, 1983](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib34)). While recommendations exist for leverage, strategic, and bottleneck items in traditional human-to-human negotiations, researchers have neglected non-critical items due to their low level of supply risk and low profit potential ( [Kang et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31)). Historically, it has been argued that basic purchasing practices, such as frame agreements and system contracting, are the most appropriate (e.g. [Kang et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31); [van Weele and Rozemeijer, 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62)).

However, with the advent of emerging technologies, such as AI-based chatbots, new and efficient possibilities for managing and addressing these “non-critical items” become feasible. No empirical research exists that demonstrates which negotiation approach a text-based chatbot buyer should take to non-critical spend items to achieve the best _economic outcome_, such as a [price discount](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/low-cost-strategy) or payment terms extension, and non-economic outcomes ( _psychological and relational outcomes_), such as trust, loyalty, or outcome satisfaction ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33)). We therefore address this research gap by attempting to answer the following research question:

RQ: What economic, psychological, and relational value does an AI-based chatbot in a human-to-machine negotiation provide across various spend items and negotiation approaches?

We address our research question by conducting two lab experiments with undergraduate business students and an online experiment with professional negotiators. In our studies, participants take the role of the supplier, while our custom-made chatbot based on OpenAI's ChatGPT algorithm is prompted to act as the buyer. By conducting these interactive experiments, we contribute to knowledge about the behavioral dimensions of buyer–supplier negotiations and provide pioneering insights into the emerging paradigm of buyer–supplier negotiations.

The remainder of our paper is organized as follows. First, we review the extant negotiation literature and illustrate its connection to AI-based chatbots in today's business environment by deriving our research hypothesis. Second, we introduce our research design and methodology, presenting each study and its results. Finally, we conclude with a general discussion, highlighting the academic and managerial implications of our study, as well as its limitations and potential areas for future research.

## 2\. Conceptual background and hypothesis development

### 2.1. Buyer–supplier negotiations

In [supply chains](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/supply-chain-management), negotiations between buyers and suppliers are a critical activity, as they affect collaboration and the [distribution of profits](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/distribution-of-profits) between the involved parties ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33)). Buyers and suppliers seek favorable agreements regarding multiple attributes, such as price, delivery, and payment terms, as well as potential penalty clauses and warranty conditions, by influencing one another during negotiations ( [Thomas et al., 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib58); [van Weele and Rozemeijer, 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62)). In addition to these _economic outcomes_, researchers have highlighted “ _psychological consequences_, such as satisfaction with the negotiation, and _relational consequences_, such as trust in a partner,” which are more implicit and will have an impact on the continuation of the business relationship ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33), p. 67).

The outcomes of buyer–supplier negotiations are influenced by structural and behavioral factors ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33)). Structural contextual factors include _relationship type_ ( [Kaufmann et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib32); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)), _relationship history_ ( [Thomas et al., 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib57), [2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib58)), and the _power balance_ ( [Kang et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31)) between the involved parties. In contrast, behavioral contextual factors include negotiation tactics that a buyer or supplier uses in an attempt to change the other party's behavior. While research exists on various negotiation tactics and approaches (e.g. [Thomas, 1992](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib56)), the two most well-known and researched approaches in academia are the _competitive negotiation approach_ (also called distributive negotiation) and the _collaborative negotiation approach_ (also called integrative negotiation), as illustrated in [Table 1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl1) below (e.g. [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib27); [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35); [Lewicki et al., 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib37); [Pruitt, 1983](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib50); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)).

Table 1. Overview of negotiation approaches based on the extant literature.

| Empty Cell | **Competitive** | **Collaborative** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Goal** | One-sided outcome | Mutually acceptable outcome |
| **Orientation** | Short-term | Long-term |
| **Characteristics** | One-time deal, few concessions, deceptive communication | Repeated transactions, open to concessions, and open communication |
| **Strategy** | Pushing the other party to make concessions | Establish trust and attempt to understand other party's needs |
| **Tactics** | Disruptive actions, threats, intimidation, aggressive behavior | Generate alternative solutions/find bridge solutions, clear and accurate communication |
| **Context a** **nd Benefits** | Low expectation of future dealings, one-time negotiation, great if one wants a bargain | Successful only if both parties adopt it, long-time relationship, repeat purchases |

Negotiators following a _collaborative approach_ strive to build trust and foster high levels of cooperation within their relationships by clearly communicating important pieces of information ( [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35)). According to [Graham (1986)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib23), a collaborative approach is only successful if both parties adopt it. Moreover, [Krause et al. (2006)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35) find that in the setting of _repeated purchases_ with the same party, the likelihood of both parties adopting a collaborative approach is increased. Negotiators adopting a _competitive approach_ typically use intimidation and aggressive threats to force their counterparts to make concessions. In this context, [Krause et al. (2006)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35) argue that both parties are likely to adopt a competitive approach in a _one-time negotiation_ due to the low expectation of future dealings.

With technological advancements, researchers have gradually moved from traditional face-to-face negotiations to online negotiations, thereby studying the impact of negotiation media, such as e-mail, instant messaging, and other web applications, on economic outcomes, such as price and negotiation time (see e.g. [Bazerman et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib4); [Croson, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib14); [Drolet and Morris, 1995](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib17); [Galin et al., 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib20); [Loewenstein et al., 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib39); [McGinn and Keros, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib44); [Naquin and Paulson, 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib48); [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)).

This shift toward online negotiations indicates an increased level of PSM maturity. According to [Andreasen and Gammelgaard (2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib3), p. 151) “maturity models are a common approach to explaining and understanding the [professional development](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/professional-development) required to change and achieve sophisticated PSM practices.” The varying levels of PSM maturity, which are shaped by factors such as organizational size, [industry](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/industry) sector, and competitive pressures, are critical in determining how companies approach negotiation strategies and integrate emerging digital technologies ( [Schiele, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib54); [van Weele and Rozemeijer, 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62)).

According to extant literature on PSM maturity models ( [Schiele, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib54); [van Weele and Rozemeijer, 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62)), in relatively immature stages, PSM is described as primarily transactional, reactive, and focused on immediate needs, with limited strategic input. In such cases, negotiations are mainly price focused and driven by cost savings. When PSM involves standardized processes, with some emphasis on supplier performance management, negotiators may still prioritize costs (e.g., price and payment terms) but begin considering quality- and delivery-related (e.g., delivery reliability) factors as well. When PSM reaches mature stages, it becomes recognized as a strategic function, influencing broader business goals, such as growth, sustainability, profitability, and innovation. Negotiations are then expected to become sophisticated and integrative in an attempt to secure long-term value through collaborative partnerships, rather than focusing solely on price and arm's length relationships. In the most mature stages, PSM is fully embedded in organizational strategy, leveraging advanced digital technologies (for analyzing supply market patterns, identifying shared interests, and facilitating transparent communications) and data-driven insights to enhance negotiation efficiency. Negotiations are highly collaborative and involve a search for continuous improvement and innovation regarding key suppliers. In contrast, immature [PSM organizations](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/management) may adopt chatbots more cautiously, aligning them with simpler negotiation strategies and streamlining distributive negotiation tasks, such as information gathering or initial price discussions ( [Úbeda et al., 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib60)).

This PSM maturity perspective allows for a nuanced understanding of how chatbots can be strategically employed within diverse buyer-supplier contexts. [Beske-Janssen et al. (2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib5), p. 8) find that negotiation skills are becoming less important for buyers because today, algorithms and digital solutions can “run requests for proposals, check supplier offers, track risks and even negotiate automatically.” It remains unknown, however, to what extent we can delegate negotiations to digital systems and whether these systems are as effective as humans in ensuring the necessary levels of trust while negotiating for improved contract terms.

While substantial attention has been paid to the economic outcomes of negotiations in various settings (i.e., media), psychological and relational outcomes, including outcome satisfaction and the desire for future interaction, are equally important and have also been studied in this context. However, findings comparing face-to-face negotiations with various e-negotiation media (e.g., email, computer chat, and video conferencing) have been somewhat contradictory. While there are mixed results regarding price, as an economic outcome, after adopting various negotiation media (see e.g. [Croson, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib14); [Galin et al., 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib20); [Loewenstein et al., 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib39); [McGinn and Keros, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib44); [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)), scholars generally agree that face-to-face negotiations are preferred over various e-negotiation media in terms of negotiation time, as well as psychological and relational outcomes. These include (1) outcome satisfaction ( [Naquin and Paulson, 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib48); [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)), (2) trust ( [Bazerman et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib4); [Drolet and Morris, 1995](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib17); [Naquin and Paulson, 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib48)), and (3) the desire for future negotiation interactions ( [Naquin and Paulson, 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib48)). Other relevant factors in the literature include negotiation approach, as outlined previously, and rapport ( [Bazerman et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib4); [Drolet and Morris, 1995](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib17)). [Purdy et al. (2000)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51) find a positive relationship between profit, or [price discount](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/low-cost-strategy), and a negotiation approach perceived as collaborative. ### 2.2. Negotiating over various spend categories

PSM scholars generally distinguish between spend categories, most frequently between the direct and indirect spend. The direct spend is defined as “all materials and products that are used for manufacturing a company's end products” ( [van Weele and Rozemeijer, 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62), p. 5). Conversely, the indirect spend includes all products and services necessary to support a company's operations and back-office activities. Within these two primary categories, various sub-categories can be identified, with one specific sub-category being the tail-end spend.

The tail-end spend can be explained by Pareto's law, as 80 % of the suppliers (i.e., the long tail) often account for only 20 % of the total spend of an organization ( [Braglia et al., 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib7)). While this definition is not universally applicable to each organization, research has shown that smaller organizations have a lower cap for the tail-end spend, whereas large organizations have a much higher cap for the tail-end spend ( [Abdollahnejadbarough et al., 2020](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib1)). In addition, PSM scholars found that many companies are not actively managing their tail-end spend, as this has historically been seen as inefficient. The cost of hiring more human buyers to negotiate tail-end spend items would not exceed the expected additional value (e.g. [van Hoek et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib61)). However, with technological advancements and the resulting digital solutions intended to automate or even autonomize various purchasing activities ( [Herold et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib26)), companies are increasingly attempting to actively manage their tail-end spend, as they recognize the substantial monetary value hidden in the [long tail](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/niche-marketing-strategy) (e.g. [Bretting, 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib8); [Sanders, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib52)). In this context, it is crucial to acknowledge the _purchasing portfolio_ developed by Peter [Kraljic (1983)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib34), who argues that spend items and categories can be placed in one of four quadrants based on their financial impact and supply risk that they represent.

Different purchasing strategies must be employed for each of the four quadrants (see e.g. [Kang et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31)), with the tail-end spend typically being classified into the “non-critical items” quadrant (frequently also referred to as routine products), which is characterized by low profit impact (i.e., low value items) and low supply risk (i.e., many alternative suppliers), encompassing items such as office supplies or certain business services ( [Gelderman and Van Weele, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib21)). According to [van Weele and Rozemeijer (2022)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib62), “the costs of handling are higher than the value of the \[non-critical\] products itself. It is not uncommon that 80 per cent of the time and efforts of a procurement department is consumed by these products” (p.110). Drawing from the traditional human-to-human negotiation literature, [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) investigate how sourcing professionals apply appropriate negotiation approaches across the KPM quadrants. Interestingly, the authors exclude non-critical items, as they argue that these do “not require serious negotiation efforts because of low level of supply risk and profit potential” (p.2344) and basic procurement practices are applied. It is therefore frequently argued that the process of sourcing these products should be organized as efficiently as possible, such as by pursuing _system contracts/framework agreements_ (e.g., for office supplies, cleaning products, and catering) and working with _e-procurement solutions_ (i.e., e-catalogs) for efficient self-ordering on the part of employees.

Existing AI-based chatbots are now also used in buyer-supplier negotiations, as illustrated in the case of Walmart and the chatbot provided by Pactum. Walmart, with a supply base of over 100,000 suppliers, had left about 20 % of its suppliers unmanaged, meaning that “suppliers have signed agreements with cookie-cutter terms that are often not negotiated” ( [van Hoek et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib61), p. 1). The reason for this is the fact that the costs of hiring more human buyers to negotiate this tail-end spend would have exceeded any additional value to be gained. Walmart's AI negotiation chatbot achieved 3 % average savings on the tail-end spend while extending payment terms to 35 days.

While the Walmart example illustrates the evolving opportunities that AI offers in terms of addressing various spend items, the existing PSM literature lacks detailed insights into the use of emerging chatbot technology in negotiations, specifically on the use of different negotiation approaches for different spend items. As with the leverage items of the KPM, _non-critical items_ have a low supply risk, thereby making it easy for buyers to find alternative suppliers that can supply the required volume at a similar price and quality. [Narsimhan and Prasad (2016)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib49) find evidence that an increase in supply risk, such as with strategic or bottleneck items, corresponds to less competitive negotiation approaches being used as compared to the low-supply-risk quadrants. Existing research suggests a more competitive negotiation approach, such as leveraging buying power, when managing items with a low supply risk, such as non-critical items ( [Kang et al., 2018](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31); [Narsimhan and Prasad, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib49)). This suggests the following hypothesis.

**H1**

When negotiating for a non-critical item with a human supplier, a chatbot (buyer) employing a competitive negotiation approach will achieve a better **price** (H1a), better **payment terms** (H1b), better **delivery terms** (H1c), and a shorter **negotiation length** (H1d) as compared to one employing a collaborative negotiation approach in the same setting.

In contrast to non-critical items, bottleneck items are characterized by low profit impact and high supply risk. The extant literature therefore argues that suppliers have a more dominant power position for these products and the purchasing strategy must thus focus on ensuring supply, even, if necessary, at an additional cost ( [Caniëls and Gelderman, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib10)). Buyers can either accept dependency and pay more or reduce the risk by modifying specifications and/or searching for substitutes to enable alternative suppliers ( [Caniëls and Gelderman, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib9)). Overall, scholars agree that the relative power lies with the supplier, and therefore, in line with findings of [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) regarding human-to-human negotiations for bottleneck items, we hypothesize as follows.

**H2**

When negotiating for a bottleneck item with a human supplier, a chatbot (buyer) employing a collaborative negotiation approach will achieve a better price (H2a), better payment terms (H2b), better delivery terms (H2c), and shorter negotiation length (H2d) as compared to one employing a competitive negotiation approach in the same setting.

While the two hypotheses above assume the perspective of the buying organization by illustrating the _economic outcome_ of the negotiation, it is also worthwhile to study _psychological_ and _relational outcomes_, such as trust, outcome satisfaction, and the desire for future interaction, that the chosen negotiation approach has on the supplier ( [Kaufmann et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib33)). Researchers have studied how various negotiation media (face-to-face, video, and email) affect psychological and relational outcomes. The results indicate that media richness matters: online negotiations are characterized by lower levels of trust as compared to face-to-face negotiations ( [Ahearne et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib2)). In this context, experimental research conducted by [Purdy et al. (2000)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51) on human-to-human negotiations using various negotiation media and negotiation approaches (competitive and collaborative), demonstrate a higher outcome satisfaction and a stronger desire for future interaction when a collaborative approach is taken, regardless of the negotiation medium. We build on these findings and predict that they will also be applicable to a human-to-machine negotiation setting: a collaborative negotiation approach on the part of the chatbot (buyer) will lead to better _psychological_ and _relational outcomes_, disregarding the spend item (non-critical or bottleneck). This suggests the following hypothesis.

**H3**

When negotiating with a human supplier, a chatbot (buyer) employing a collaborative negotiation approach will lead to higher trust (H3a), higher outcome satisfaction (H3b), and a stronger desire for future interaction (H3c) on the part of the supplier as compared to employing a competitive negotiation approach in the same setting.

## 3\. Methodology

To test our research hypotheses, we conducted a behavioral experiment which is a strong method to “investigate the world of factors influencing human judgement and decision-making” ( [Eckerd, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib19), p. 258) by being able to directly observe the impact of a change in a factor (i.e. manipulation) on an outcome. We conducted a series of experiments to empirically test our hypothesis and replicate and validate the initial findings. Academic staff (PhD students, professors, and lecturers) participated in a pre-test of our study design. During this testing phase, the instructions were modified based on their feedback, and the time required for the experiment, including the negotiation time needed, was determined. Because the participants only learned about the item that they negotiated over, the content was limited to a short description of the item: the time period of 15 min is thus an experimental limitation, and we acknowledge that negotiations are often longer and not based on a one-time interaction.

After our pre-test, we began with a student sample (Study 1) to verify the effectiveness of our manipulations and evaluate the functionality of the online negotiation setting using a self-built chat interface based on Open AI's GPT model 3.5-turbo. While working on this, we became aware of research pointing toward the variable performance of ChatGPT ( [Chen et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib12)), which is why we conducted Study 2—a full replication of Study 1. Following the approach of existing PSM research on experiments, we chose these two student samples, as it was a cost-effective method of initial hypothesis testing and experimental validation ( [Eckerd, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib19)). Moreover, we opted for large samples to increase the statistical power of the results ( [Carter et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib11)). After we confirmed with the first two studies, that the online chat interface functioned as intended, we conducted a large-scale online study with B2B negotiation professionals in our network (Study 3). ### 3.1. Design and procedure

In all three studies, we tested our hypothesis by employing a 2 (negotiation approach: collaborative versus competitive) × 2 (item type: non-critical versus bottleneck) between-subjects experiment. In Studies 1 and 2, undergraduate business students from a large Dutch public university participated and received course credit for attending the experiment, which was conducted on desktop computers in the university lab. In contrast, our main study, which is Study 3, incorporates practitioners with a procurement or sales background who are experienced in buyer–supplier negotiations to ensure the validity of our findings, learn how experienced negotiators may perform, and understand their perceptions of the negotiation interaction with the chatbot. Moreover, Study 3 differs due to the mostly remote data collection setup, as roughly two-thirds of respondents participated online, as compared to the students being in the lab, whereas one-third participated in an in-class guided experiment as part of executive education workshops. No monetary incentives were given, but the participants were assured that the study's results would be shared after completion.

All the studies adhered to the same standardized procedure. Initially, the participants were directed to a survey page, on which they provided their informed consent. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions, received background information on the negotiation task, and were subsequently directed to a chat interface, initiating the negotiation process. Participants assumed the role of suppliers negotiating with a buyer company for a contract renewal (a straight rebuy). The items under negotiation varied by condition: standardized office desks in the non-critical item condition and customized IT hardware (i.e., powerbanks) in the bottleneck condition. The buyer is represented by an AI-based chatbot, which we named ProcureBot Charlie, hereafter simply Charlie, with which the participants negotiated via a web-based chat interface (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1) for an illustration). Participants were made aware that they were negotiating with a non-human counterpart in the introduction text of the study, as well as verbally (“ProcureBot”) and graphically by illustrating Charlie as an AI-based chatbot (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). Charlie was based on OpenAI's GPT-3 model (GPT-3.5-turbo), which we primed with background information and prompts for each of the four group conditions ( [Appendix B](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). In each of the four conditions, Charlie was asked to reach a 10 % price discount and increase the payment terms to ten days. All other contract items, such as delivery terms and quantity, were left open and could be flexibly addressed by both parties. For the sake of simplicity, the key information within the negotiation assignment for each group was summarized on the chat interface (see also [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). After the assigned time period ended (maximum 15 min), the participants were asked to end the negotiation and return to the survey page. In a follow-up survey, the participants were asked to share their negotiation experience (e.g. whether they reached an agreement and, if so, which terms were agreed upon, i.e., _economic outcomes_). Additionally, questions related to subjective perceptions about the outcomes (i.e., _psychological and relational outcomes_) were asked.

We applied the same set of prespecified quality criteria across all studies. Participants with incomplete responses were excluded, as were those who failed the attention check. Additionally, negotiations that were too short to yield a meaningful outcome were excluded, with too short being defined as negotiations that were 1.5 [standard deviations](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/measure-of-dispersion) below the mean negotiation length. ### 3.2. Measures

While _economic outcomes_ were directly visible via the negotiation interactions on the chat screen, _psychological_ and _relational outcomes_ were measured using a follow-up survey with established scales. To measure _trust_, both dependability and benevolence, from the suppliers' perspective, we adapted the eight items created by [Hill et al. (2009)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib28). Moreover, we assessed the _outcome satisfaction_ of the supplier (human) with a four-item measure created by [Yao and Storme (2021)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib63). Lastly, we measure _desire for future interaction_ with a two-item measure found in [Jap (2007)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib30). Participants responded to all measures on a 7-point [Likert scale](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/likert-scale) (from strongly disagree = 1 to strongly agree = 7). We provide the items for all constructs, including reliability statistics (i.e., Cronbach's Alpha), in [Appendix C](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1).

### 3.3. Analytical approach

To support the validation of our studies, we conduct manipulation checks to “assess whether participants are interpreting the experimental treatments as intended and portrayed by the researchers” ( [Eckerd, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib19), p. 260). To check the success of our two manipulations, we asked the participants to rate two measures. For item type, we used two single-item measures (1. Non-Critical Item: “I represented a supplier of a non-critical item (low profit impact and low supply risk/complexity)”; 2. Bottleneck Item: “I represented a supplier of a bottleneck item (low profit impact and high supply risk/complexity)”) rated on a 7-point Likert scale (from strongly disagree = 1 to strongly agree = 7). As intended, the participants in the office desk condition perceived the item in question as a non-critical item, whereas the participants in the powerbank condition perceived it as a bottleneck item.

We used the characteristics presented in [Table 1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl1) to contrast the two negotiation approaches. Using 7-point questions on a semantic-differential scale, participants were asked to indicate whether they perceived the negotiation chatbot to be 1. “very collaborative” versus “very competitive”; 2. “very friendly” versus “very aggressive”; 3. “communicating very openly” versus “communicating very deceptively (using threats)”; and 4. “interested in a very mutually acceptable outcome” versus “interested in a very one-sided outcome (selfish)”. Participants rated the chatbot as more collaborative in the two collaborative conditions as compared to the two competitive conditions, confirming our intended manipulation. We provide the analysis of our two manipulation checks in [Appendix D](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1).

To analyze our data, we used IBM's Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) Software, Version 29. To test interaction effects of our hypothesis, the PROCESS macro developed by [Hayes (2017)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib25) – model 1 is a suitable tool. Additionally, for individual relationships between variables, we used the General Linear Model (GLM) to calculate means as well as effect sizes (see [Appendix E](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)).

In addition to the statistical analysis, we also performed [language analysis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/language-analysis) using the latest version of the linguistic inquiry and word count (LIWC-22) software program to conduct our text analysis ( [Boyd et al., 2022](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib6)). To do so, we proceeded to analyze the data derived from the chat interaction between our study participants and Charlie. We analyze the practitioners’ interactions in Study 3, which, given the practitioner sample, should provide the best understanding of such interactions in practice.

### 4.2. Language analysis

Using LIWC, we analyzed suppliers' (i.e. human participants’) word counts when interacting with collaborative versus competitive chatbots. Given a collaborative negotiation approach, communication is more elaborate because of asking for information, summarizing information, or paraphrasing for the sake of clarification ( [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib27)), which is reflected in our prompting for Charlie (see [Appendix B](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). We hypothesized that suppliers interacting with the collaborative-prompted chatbot would exhibit more elaborate communication patterns as compared to those facing the competitive-prompted version. To calculate the word counts, we uploaded an Excel file with the chat interactions between the participants and Charlie and received a word count for each participant. We then used the GLM in SPSS to conduct an analysis based on the four group conditions. Overall, we do not find differences in the four group conditions, implying that suppliers do not use more words when negotiating with a competitively prompted chatbot versus a collaboratively prompted chatbot or when the item type under negotiation is non-critical versus bottleneck.

Secondly, we employed language-style-matching (LSM) metrics to quantify linguistic synchronization between the human suppliers and the chatbot buyer on a scale of 0–1. This analysis examined whether participants’ communication patterns were aligned with either negotiation approach based on the functional word usage patterns (pronouns, articles, and prepositions) between the conversational parties ( [Gonzales et al., 2010](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib22)). To calculate LSM, we again uploaded the Excel file with the negotiation interactions between the participants and Charlie to LIWC for analysis ( [Gonzales et al., 2010](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib22)). We find a significant effect regarding negotiation approach: higher LSM scores (i.e., higher similarity) in chat interactions in which a competitively promoted chatbot is employed, which implies that suppliers also used more aggressive and threating language.
