## 5\. Discussion

The results of our three studies provide evidence for the usability and value of AI-based chatbots in buyer–supplier negotiations. More specifically, we build upon established research on different negotiation approaches in a human-to-human context (i.e. [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib64)) and illustrate distinct performance outcomes (economic as well as psychological and relational) in a human-to-machine setting. While the findings did not confirm the interaction effects in question (H1 and H2), they confirmed that a competitively prompted chatbot leads to a higher price discount for the buying organization across all studies and a quicker negotiation duration as compared to a chatbot employing a collaborative negotiation approach (Studies 1 and 2). Suppliers trust the collaborative negotiation approach of the chatbot more fully and show higher outcome satisfaction, as well as a stronger desire for future interaction (across all studies) with this approach.

First, we find a significant effect for price discounts in all three studies: the chatbot achieved higher price discounts when it employed a competitive negotiation approach, disregarding item type (non-critical or bottleneck). When comparing the results regarding price discount across all three studies, we find that the chatbot achieved substantial savings, coming very close to the prompted goal of 10 % in both student samples (Studies 1 and 2). However, significantly lower savings (see [Appendix E](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1): between 1,1 % and 5,5 %) were achieved when negotiating with experienced negotiators (Study 3). Our findings regarding price discount contradict the previous findings of [Purdy et al. (2000)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51), who found a positive relationship between price discount and a (perceived) collaborative negotiation approach in a human-to-human negotiation setting. The contradicting findings can be explained by the fact a collaborative negotiation approach is mostly used and effective in repeated purchases with the same party ( [Krause et al., 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35)). While the negotiation task in our study was described as a contract renewal (i.e. repeated purchase), participants essentially negotiated with the supplier (i.e. Charlie) for the first time and hence the interaction could have been perceived as a one-time negotiation with low expectation of future dealings – thereby explaining the superior performance of a competitive negotiation approach according to [Krause et al. (2006)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib35).

Second, we find a significant effect on payment terms in our study with practitioners (Study 3): better payment terms for the buyer were achieved when the chatbot employed a competitive negotiation approach. While undergraduate students may possess foundational knowledge of various contract items, they may not be able to effectively integrate and make tradeoffs between multiple contract terms during negotiations, thereby often prioritizing price. Also, unlike students, experienced practitioners often better understand the direct financial impact of changing payment terms and are often more experienced in conducting multi-attribute negotiations. This may account for the more significant effect on payment terms observed in our practitioner study (Study 3) as compared to our student studies (Studies 1 and 2). Especially, [supply chain](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/supply-chain-management)[finance](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/finance) research has considered payment terms in conjunction with other contractual terms such as order quantity (see e.g. [Li et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib38)) which illustrates this multi-attribute nature of negotiations and hence the advantage of experience in negotiations.

Third, we find a significant effect on negotiation duration. When faced with a competitively prompted chatbot, students conducted shorter negotiations as compared to practitioners, who might be less likely to shy away from assertive negotiation counterparts. When analyzing the chat interactions, we found that practitioners are inclined to find creative ways to convince the chatbot that a price discount of 10 % and/or an extension [of payment terms](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/terms-and-conditions) may not be feasible by referring for instance to the tough economic environment (i.e. inflation). Students, on the other hand, settle more quickly when faced with a competitively prompted chatbot and seem to be more easily intimidated by it. We observe that our student samples more frequently came to an agreement when pushed by a competitively prompted chatbot as compared to practitioners (see [Table 4](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl4) above). We therefore extent existing body of literature that has shown that negotiation experience matters in fostering negotiation performance (see e.g. [Lumineau and Henderson, 2012](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib40); [Moran and Ritov, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib47); [Thompson, 1990](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib59))

Fourth, in addition to the economic outcomes, psychological and relational outcomes were measured through existing scales. In all three studies, we find significant effects for negotiation approach. Respondents indicated higher trust, higher outcome satisfaction, and a stronger desire for future interaction when facing a collaboratively prompted chatbot (versus a competitively prompted chatbot). We can therefore contribute to existing research on B2B negotiations between human buyers and suppliers ( [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)) and highlight the fact that this also holds for interactions between a human and an AI-based chatbot. In our study with practitioners (Study 3), we further find significant effects for item type: when a bottleneck item was negotiated, regardless of the negotiation approach, respondents indicated higher trust (benevolence) as compared to interactions in which a non-critical item was negotiated (see [Table 5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl5)). We therefore extend findings of [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) on human-to-human negotiations for different quadrants of the KPM by illustrating the necessity to consider the item type (and hence the power position of the buyer) and the resulting effect on trust as a negotiation outcome.

Fifth, as the verbal interactions between the partitioners and Charlie might be most realistic, we also conducted language analysis using LIWC software and the data derived from Study 3. Text analysis using LIWC software indicated that more similar communication styles between practitioners and the chatbot were prevalent when the chatbot used a competitive negotiation approach, while an analysis of the word count showed no substantial differences in the numbers of words used between the four group conditions.

## 6\. Conclusion

With the advent of technology, firms are increasingly employing AI-based chatbots in their processes. While research in other fields, such as marketing or sales, has already highlighted evidence for their success and usage, chatbots are currently an under-researched topic in the field of PSM. By conducting three experiments with undergraduate students, as well as experienced buyer-supplier negotiation professionals, we provide initial insights into how the negotiations of the future might look like and what the important _outcome-influencing factors_, both structural and behavioral, might be in this regard. This section will elaborate on the academic and managerial implications and then provide the limitations and future research avenues.

### 6.1. Academic implications

We contribute to contemporary knowledge about buyer–supplier negotiations in multiple ways. First, while research on AI in the field of PSM is increasing (e.g. [Guida et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib24); [Spreitzenbarth et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib55)), to our knowledge, this is the first study to test various _outcome-influencing factors_ (structural and behavioral) in negotiations between AI-based chatbots (buyers) and humans (suppliers). By drawing on existing research on outcome-influencing factors, such as the _negotiation approach_ or the _power balance_ (operationalized as spend item) in a human-to-human negotiation setting (see [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl2)), we provide novel insights into a human-to-machine negotiation setting. We extend previous work by [Kang et al. (2018)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib31) and demonstrate that AI-based chatbots provide value in various negotiation settings.

Second, we use experiments. This method is nascent in supply chain management ( [Carter et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib11)) and PSM research ( [Eckerd, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib19)). With three experimental studies using a between-subjects design and both student and practitioner samples, we advance the understanding of the behavioral dimensions of buyer–supplier negotiations and provide pioneering insights into the future landscape of buyer–supplier negotiations. Our findings demonstrate that the experimental results are consistent between student and practitioner samples, confirming the validity of using student samples to test hypotheses, a practice supported in disciplines such as psychology and marketing. This implies that future PSM research could rely more heavily on the use of student samples to explore complex negotiation dynamics, thus broadening the scope and feasibility of experimental designs. This could promote incorporating more behavioral and experimental approaches into PSM research to further inform the development of nuanced theories that account for psychological and relational factors in buyer–supplier interactions. Additionally, our work can allow future PSM studies to explore the impacts of GAI in these negotiations, providing a framework for examining the constantly evolving nature of buyer–supplier engagements.

### 6.2. Managerial implications

We also contribute to practice, as our study provides initial insights into how GAI can be leveraged for efficient buyer–supplier negotiations and two main managerial implications for professionals can be drawn from it. First, our results provide evidence on the _outcome-influencing factors_ regarding an AI-based chatbot in buyer–supplier negotiations, such as negotiation approach and item type. Our overall results indicate that buying organizations, or, rather, Chief Procurement Officers (CPOs) wishing to implement a negotiation chatbot must make a trade-off: higher _economic outcomes_ for one's own organization versus higher trust, outcome satisfaction, and desire for future interaction on the part of the counterpart (supplier), depending on which negotiation approach the chatbot will employ.

Second, while generative AI chatbots demonstrate effectiveness in controlled settings, they are not yet suitable for autonomous buyer–supplier negotiations at scale. However, they can effectively support specific negotiation tasks, while purpose-built AI negotiation tools are better suited for full-scale implementation. Similar to research by [Dinnar et al. (2021)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib16) on the use of AI in teaching negotiations, we see the value of our negotiation interface based on ChatGPT for negotiation training purposes. The prompts feeding ChatGPT can easily be adapted, which makes it possible to quickly develop and tailor training cases to mimic specific negotiation needs and contexts. This also enables buyers to perform one or more trial runs to prepare for an upcoming complex negotiation. Thus, AI-powered negotiation chatbots provide companies with a cost-efficient and effective approach to training employees and preparing them for upcoming negotiations.

### 6.3. Limitations and further research

Our research has several limitations that offer opportunities for future study. The first concerns our sample composition. While we initially tested our manipulations and setting with students who had limited negotiation experience, our main study focused on practitioners that are experienced in buyer-supplier negotiations. While we believe that our practitioner sample is representative, we are aware of some weaknesses, such as (1) data collection being performed online and partially remotely, (2) the sample being of average size, and (3) the participants residing in multiple countries that met the WEIRD (Western, educated, industrial, rich, and democratic) criteria ( [Carter et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib11)). Future research could replicate Study 3 with a larger practitioner sample in a guided in-person setting and with non-WEIRD participants. In this way, cross-cultural comparisons can be conducted.

A second limitation concerns our manipulations. We thoroughly tested our manipulations and found significant effects in all three studies, as indicated above. While our study is intended to provide initial insights into the negotiations of the future, further improvements in the operationalization of our manipulations, as well as development of further manipulations (i.e., contextual factors, such as relational type or relational history), as shown in [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#tbl2), could be valuable next steps. In addition, we acknowledge that negotiations are often longer than 15 min and not based on a one-time interaction. Future researchers could address these issues by conducting multi-round negotiations in which switching between negotiation approaches is possible. This is described as “strategic adaptability” by [Heunis et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib27). This would simulate real buyer-supplier negotiations as closely as possible.

The third limitation concerns the comparability of the results. Extant research has found that “communication media can have a significant impact on negotiations” ( [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51), p. 162). While human-to-machine interactions are increasing in popularity, it would have been ideal to also compare these results ( _economic outcomes_ and _psychological and relational outcomes_) with online chat interactions between two humans and thus contribute to the existing knowledge on negotiation medium ( [Croson, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib14); [Galin et al., 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib20); [Loewenstein et al., 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib39); [McGinn and Keros, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib44); [Purdy et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#bib51)).

While our use of [large language models](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/large-language-model) (OpenAI's ChatGPT) as the backend system revealed certain limitations of these models, notably their tendency to concede when challenged, this characteristic illuminates a crucial research frontier. Though this behavior created valuable training opportunities for negotiation skills development, it also highlights the need to explore how various AI architectures maintain negotiation positions under pressure. Future research using alternative AI systems could not only test model resilience but also help define the characteristics needed for AI to become a truly effective negotiation partner. As (procurement) organizations continue to integrate AI into their operations, understanding these dynamics will be essential for successfully merging AI within PSM and negotiation practices.

## Appendix E. Summary of the experiment plan

| EXPERIMENT PLAN |
| --- |
| **Design and Procedure** |
| - ⁃<br>  **Setting:** Employing a 2 (negotiation approach: collaborative vs. competitive) × 2 (item type: non-critical vs. bottleneck) between-subject experiment.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Sample:**<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  Study 1 and study 2: undergraduate business students from a large Dutch public university participated and received course credit for attending the experiment conducted on desktop computers in the university lab.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  Study 3: incorporates practitioners that work within procurement or sales to ensure validity of our findings, to learn about how participants with negotiation experience might perform, and to understand their perception of the negotiation interaction with the chatbot. Moreover, Study 3 differs due to the (mostly) remote set-up of data collection as roughly two-thirds of respondents participated online (compared students being in the lab) whereas one-third participated in an in-class guided experiment as part of procurement workshops. No monetary incentive was given but the assurance that the study's results would be shared after completion.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Procedure:** All studies adhered to the same standardized procedure. Initially, participants were directed to a survey page, where they provided their informed consent. Participants were then randomly assigned to one of four experimental conditions, received background information on the negotiation task and were subsequently directed to a chat interface, initiating the negotiation process. Participants assumed the role of suppliers negotiating with a buyer-company for contract renewal (straight-rebuy). The items under negotiation varied by condition: standardized office desks in the non-critical item condition and customized powerbanks in the bottleneck condition. The buyer is represented by an AI-based chatbot which we named “ProcureBot Charlie” with which participants negotiate via a web-based chat interface (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1) for an illustration). Participants were made aware that they were negotiating with a non-human counterpart in the introduction text of the study as well as by verbally (“ProcureBot”) and graphically illustrating Charlie as an AI-based chatbot (see [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). Charlie was based on OpenAI's GPT-3 model (Model: GPT-3.5-turbo), which is primed with background information and prompts for each of the four group conditions (see [Appendix B](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). In each of the four different conditions, ChatGPT was asked to reach a ten percent price discount and increase payment terms to ten days. All other contract items such as delivery terms or quantity were left open and could be flexibly addressed by both parties. For simplicity, key information of the negotiation assignment for each group was summarized on the chat interface (see also [Appendix A](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409225000214#appsec1)). Once the negotiation finished (maximum 15 min), participants were asked to end the negotiation and return to the survey page. In a second survey, participants were then asked to share their negotiation experience e.g. whether they reached agreement and if so, which terms were agreed upon (i.e. _economic outcomes_). Additionally, questions related to subjective perceptions (i.e. _psychological and relational outcomes_) about the outcomes were asked.<br>  <br>- ⁃<br>  **Quality Criteria:** same set of prespecified quality criteria across all studies. Participants with incomplete responses were excluded, as were those who failed the attention check. Additionally, negotiations that were too short to yield a meaningful outcome were excluded, with "too short" defined as negotiations that were 1.5 standard deviations below the mean negotiation length. ## Abstract

Strategic adaptability -a key competency in Purchasing and Supply Management- is the ability to switch between integrative and distributive negotiation strategies when needed. Although its importance has been widely recognized, there remains a notable absence of dedicated training specifically designed to educate Purchasing and Supply Management students and professionals in recognizing and applying strategic adaptability during negotiations. This paper introduces a training program to fill this gap. At its core, the training utilizes a blend of educational learning methods, including [observational learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/observational-learning). It features short video clips of condensed negotiation scenarios, which provide practical insights into strategy adjustments and their effects. Feedback from students supports the engagement and efficacy of this multi-method training approach. Aiding its practical implementation, all materials are freely accessible and can be found in the [Supplementary materials](https://doi.org/10.17026/SS/OVS5DE).

## 1\. Introduction

Negotiation is an essential skill that is transferable to many professional contexts and highly valued by employers ( [Beske-Janssen et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib7); [Danao, 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib18); [European Labour Authority, 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib24)). Especially in the purchasing and supply management (PSM) domain, negotiation skills can help to strengthen buyer-supplier relationships and achieve strategic partnerships ( [Spekman, 1988](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib79); [Jap, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib36); [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3)). Hence, it is no surprise that negotiation skills are generally classified among the most important skills for PSM professionals ( [Thomas et al., 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib86); [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3)) and are mentioned in 73% of the studies on PSM skills ( [Stek and Schiele, 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib82)). Negotiation skills are needed both internally in the organization, such as within teams and in communications with other departments ( [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3)), as well as externally in the buyer-supplier interface ( [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73)). As such, negotiations in the context of PSM extend beyond mere cost savings ( [Murfield et al., 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib57)) and may focus on innovation instead ( [Lintukangas et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib48)). However, despite its importance, negotiation education has not received much attention in the PSM literature, revealing a significant gap in professionals' understanding of negotiation strategies ( [Kharbanda and Stallworthy, 1991](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib38); [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77); [Ramsay, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68)).

In this paper, we present a negotiation training specifically focusing on strategic adaptability. Strategic adaptability is the competence to apply both integrative and distributive negotiation strategies. _The integrative strategy_ is also known as a collaborative win-win approach, focusing on value creation, and the _distributive strategy_ as a competitive win-lose approach, focusing on value claiming ( [Walton and McKersie, 1965](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib95); [Deutsch, 1973](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib19); [Lax and Sebenius, 1986](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib44); [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73)). Strategic adaptability in negotiation refers to using a repertoire of integrative and distributive strategies and switching between these when needed. Such a need may arise from cues on the content, opponent, process, or context level ( [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). Despite its relevance, adaptability in negotiations is argued to belong to the least explored and developed competencies ( [Roloff et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib72); [Wheeler, 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib100)). Our training enables negotiation students to engage in authentic scenarios and learn through observation, active participation, and interactive engagement. In doing so, we follow recommendations by the education literature suggesting a positive impact of [observational learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/observational-learning) where students act as analysts by observing behaviors and strategies and turning these insights into their own actions ( [Nadler et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib58); [Chapman et al., 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib16)). We present an engaging, multi-method training based on an instructional design approach, combining different learning theories. Central to the training is an [observational learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/observational-learning) exercise. For this purpose, we developed short video clips demonstrating negotiation strategies and strategic adaptability cues.

This paper offers two main contributions. First, it introduces the first training focused on dynamic negotiation processes and strategic adaptability, drawing from established negotiation concepts ( [Walton and McKersie, 1965](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib95); [Druckman, 2001](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib20); [Olekalns and Smith, 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib61); [Olekalns and Weingart, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib62)). Despite the recognized importance of strategic adaptability, there are limited guidelines for training in this area ( [Putnam and Powers, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib67); [Chapman et al., 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib16); [Preuss and van der Wijst, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65); [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). Educators and trainers can incorporate this training into their curricula using our educational design process and learning methods. Second, while our focus is on negotiation strategies, the training has broader applications within the PSM domain, linking to concepts such as pie expansion, power and trust in B2B negotiations, buyer-supplier satisfaction, and preparation ( [Spekman, 1988](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib79); [Jap, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib36); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib101); [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3); [Ried et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib71)). This highlights that learning about adaptability not only enhances negotiation strategies but also has wider implications for the field of PSM.

Below, we first discuss the relevant PSM and negotiation literature before introducing our strategic adaptability negotiation training. The training is based on four blocks, and all teaching materials are included. We validate the proof of concept based on students' evaluation and provide suggestions on how educators can incorporate this training into the course curriculum. The paper concludes with a discussion on the application of the training and how it can add value in the broader PSM context.

## 2\. Literature review

### 2.1. Negotiations and the PSM literature

Negotiation is a crucial task for purchasers ( [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77)). Similar to the negotiation literature, the PSM literature distinguishes between integrative and distributive strategies (e.g., see [Ramsay, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68); [Ramsay, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib69); [Kelly and Chicksand, 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib37)). The integrative negotiation approach is grounded in the assumption that the interests of the parties are not completely opposed and that cooperation can lead to mutual benefits, maximizing joint value. It requires open discussion and free information exchange ( [Ramsay, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68)). Integrative strategies consist of tactics where value is created through reciprocation and ensuring that the interests of all parties are satisfied. This can be done, for instance, by asking and sharing information across all issues honestly, summarizing for clarification, or making multi-issue offers and collaborative statements ( [Weingart et al., 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib97)). In contrast, the distributive negotiation approach focuses on the opposing interests of the parties, viewing negotiation as a zero-sum game where one party's gain is the other's loss. This often reflects a more confrontational, adversarial style known as the value-claiming approach. Distributive strategies include tactics used to secure concessions and claim value at the expense of the other party ( [Fulmer and Barry, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib29)). For instance, by asking or sharing information one issue at a time, making single-issue offers, substantiating the position, or using deception ( [Weingart et al., 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib97)). This strategy can also include haggling, also referred to as bargaining, involving back-and-forth discussions about one issue ( [Kelly and Chicksand, 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib37)). [Table 1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#tbl1) provides an overview of these negotiation behaviors and communication examples for each strategy.

Table 1. Negotiation strategies and their common behaviors, including communication examples.

| Negotiation strategy | Negotiation behavior | Communication example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integrative | Asking for or sharing information about interests and priorities across all issues honestly and exploratively. | “What concerns do you have about the property?” |
| Summarizing or paraphrasing for clarification and to gain more insights and understanding. | “If I understand correctly, you're saying that … ?” |
| Making multi-issue offers, logrolling, or package deals. | “I offer €380,000 for the property, considering the market condition. However, we are flexible on the moving date …” |
| Collaborative, progress seeking or relationship building statements. | “I believe we can work together to find a solution that benefits both of us. I want to ensure that we reach an agreement that satisfies both your needs and mine.” |
| Distributive | Asking for information about or discussing position, facts, or bottom line one issue at a time. | "I appreciate your perspective, but this does not work for me. Can you lower the price to meet my terms?" |
| Making an offer for one issue at a time, proposing one-sided concessions, or suggesting solutions to meet own interests. | "I want €400,000 for the property." |
| Substantiating position or persuasive statements. | "The property is not worth more because … " |
| Using deception, lies, time pressure, referring to power, misrepresentation, ultimatums, threats, or aggressive comments. | "This is my final offer." |

The PSM literature investigates integrative and distributive strategies from different perspectives. For example, [Zachariassen (2008)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib101) shows that buyers and suppliers choose an integrative or distributive negotiation strategy based on their relationship with the other party (e.g., arm's length or strategic partnership). [Thompson (1990a)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib87) and [Ramsay (2004)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68) suggest that negotiators tend to prefer using distributive strategies in (strategic partnership) negotiations, which can be less advantageous compared to integrative strategies. [Preuss and van der Wijst (2017)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65) show that negotiators use multiple strategies in the negotiation process.

Although not always mentioned explicitly, integrative and distributive strategies align with other concepts discussed in the PSM literature. For instance, negotiators focusing on creating strategic partnerships or buyer-supplier collaborations focusing on so-called "pie expansion" align with integrative strategies where collaborative efforts result in a larger shared benefit that neither party could achieve alone ( [Spekman, 1988](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib79); [Jap, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib36)). Other studies focus on distributive strategies. For example, [Ried et al. (2023)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib71) emphasize that negotiators should pay careful attention to the effects of their behaviors, particularly regarding their level of unethical behaviors, such as deception, which can unconsciously spill over to the opponent. In another study, [Ried et al. (2021)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib70) showed that opportunistic behaviors reduce counterparts' willingness to share information, which is an important driver of collaboration and relationship performance ( [Carr and Pearson, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib15); [Cao and Zhang, 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib14)). Furthermore, [Thomas et al. (2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib86) found that distributive tactics might be tolerated in less interdependent contexts but can adversely affect the intention to share knowledge in more interconnected buyer-supplier relationships.

Negotiation strategies are also discussed in the literature on customer satisfaction. For example, [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo (2019)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73) emphasize the impact of a supplier's negotiation behavior on a customer's perceived satisfaction. They reveal that distributive strategies do not necessarily lead to negative customer satisfaction because the suppliers combine integrative and distributive strategies, supporting their complementariness. Other studies consider game theoretical approaches. [Game theory](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/game-theory) holds an important role in negotiation research ( [Spina et al., 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib80)). This theory favors linear stage models over a balanced approach between integrative and distributive strategies, often overlooking the long-term aspects of negotiations and underemphasizing relational strategies ( [Åge and Eklinder-Frick, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib1)). Furthermore, such approaches are often difficult to be applied in real-world, multi-issue negotiations ( [Herbst et al., 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib34); [Kelly and Chicksand, 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib37)).

Finally, the PSM has explored the negotiation preparation process. During these preparations, negotiators perform self-assessment, take perspective, and establish situational awareness ( [Malhotra, 2016](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib51)). For instance, [Smeltzer et al. (2003)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77) propose a six-step strategic sourcing process based on [Steele and Court (1996)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib81) and [Lewicki et al. (2000)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib47) that supports purchasers in preparing and developing a strategy for the negotiation. They conclude that professionals have difficulties in implementing suitable negotiation strategies and rather adhere to the company's supply management culture in choosing the negotiation style, ignoring the dynamic and adaptive nature of the negotiation process ( [Preuss and van der Wijst, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65); [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). Alternatively, [Fleming and Hawes (2017)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib27) introduce a negotiation [scorecard](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/balanced-scorecard), which is a planning tool to understand the negotiation context and to develop the negotiation strategy. They suggest that combining integrative and distributive strategies is recommended when entering a mixed-motive negotiation.

### 2.2. Strategic adaptability in negotiation

A simplistic dichotomous view of negotiation strategies does not adequately capture the nuances of real-world negotiations, where purely integrative and distributive behaviors are uncommon ( [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73)). A single-sided negotiation approach can lead to overlooking opportunities for creating mutual benefits and leaving value on the table, resulting in suboptimal agreements ( [Thompson, 1990b](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib88); [Thompson and Hastie, 1990](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib89); [Weingart et al., 1996](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib98)). In addition, a one-size-fits-all negotiation strategy is unrealistic because the negotiation process can be uncertain and iterative. Instead, previous studies identified that adaptation is a critical competence in negotiation and helps to attain better outcomes compared to using a single strategy ( [Walton and McKersie, 1965](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib95); [Van de Vliert et al., 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib93); [Putnam and Powers, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib67); [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73)). In line with this, [Preuss and van der Wijst (2017)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65) found that negotiators typically do not adhere to a single negotiation style but vary their approach across different phases of the negotiation process. [Buckley (2001)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib13) suggests that adopting a distributive strategy towards the end of the negotiation is frequently necessary to secure more favorable outcomes, and avoiding confrontation at this stage may result in suboptimal results. [Ramsay (2004)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68) suggests that the integrative phase logically precedes the competitive phase in mixed negotiations. However, [Heunis et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35) show that negotiations do not typically have these two phases. Instead, negotiators adapt their strategy more frequently. It is argued that negotiators should anticipate and monitor the counterpart's actions to verify and adjust their priorities and strategies ( [Savage et al., 1989](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib74)). For example, negotiations commonly involve working with incomplete information and multiple negotiation issues ( [Roloff et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib72); [Wheeler, 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib100); [Lewicki and Bruce, 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib46)), such as the supplier's production capacity or the negotiation strategy of the counterpart. This hidden information is identified during the negotiation by asking questions and sharing information. Understanding this and adapting the negotiation strategy to different situational and personal differences can assist purchasers in becoming more effective in achieving desired outcomes ( [Shell, 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib76)).

Adaptability is the ability to adjust to changing circumstances by changing own approaches to fit different environments ( [Martin et al., 2012](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib53)). The negotiation literature already examined adaptations in strategy in different fields. For instance, research on _turning points_ (e.g., see [Druckman, 2001](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib20); [Olekalns and Weingart, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib62); [Druckman and Olekalns, 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib22)) demonstrates how negotiators change their strategy based on the content, opponent, process, and context level. A different field focuses on _phase models_ (e.g., see [Olekalns et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib60); [Weingart and Olekalns, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib99)) and shows that changes in strategy can also occur as a reaction to the opponent. [Heunis et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35) combined these different “cues” in their strategic adaptability framework. This framework captures strategy changes on four levels.

First, _content-level_ adaptation occurs when the strategy changes depending on the (priority of the) issue under discussion or when new information is shared. Second, _opponent-level_ adaptation occurs when a negotiator adopts the strategy in reaction to (a strategic change of the) opponent. This can happen after the opponent shifts the strategy, to break the resistance of an opponent not changing strategy, or to better understand the opponent. Third, _process-level_ adaptation occurs when the negotiation parties are stuck in the negotiation process. This commonly occurs when facing a [deadlock](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/deadlock). Fourth, _context-level_ adaptation occurs when perceptions or priorities change due to external factors (including policy or leadership changes or the inclusion of third parties). A change in context can affect the negotiator's initial strategy, leading to a strategic adaptation. [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#tbl2) presents these four categories and the cues leading to strategic adaptations, each instrumental in directing strategic change. Our training, which we present below, builds on these adaptability categories and helps students learn to monitor the negotiation process and recognize and respond to these cues.

Table 2. Strategic adaptability cues on the content, opponent, process, and context level.

| **CONTENT LEVEL** | **PROCESS LEVEL** |
| --- | --- |
| Adapting strategy depending on the issue under discussion (e.g., when changing to an issue with a different priority level). | Changing strategy after being stuck in negotiation process (e.g., deadlock). |
| **OPPONENT LEVEL** | **CONTEXT LEVEL** |
| Align strategy to opponent, or adapting to opponent's strategy change (e.g., due to resistance, or to understand opponent). | Perceptions or priorities change because of external factors (e.g., policy or leadership changes or inclusion of third parties). |

| _Purpose:_ This video shows how opposing negotiation behaviors can influence the negotiation process during a contract renewal. The buyer and supplier enter a "tit-for-tat" spiral where no progress seems possible until the supplier recognizes the deadlock. The video ends with both parties using integrative behaviors to find a solution. | ![Image 1](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409224000773-fx1.jpg)<br>_Key cues:_ Opponent-, and process-based adaptations<br>_Duration:_ 3:54 min |

The buyer and supplier move quickly to distributive behaviors and miss opportunities to adapt strategies, resulting in suboptimal agreement terms. | ![Image 3](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409224000773-fx3.jpg)<br>_Key cues:_ Missed adaptations (content-, and opponent based)<br>_Duration:_ 3:25 min |

The buyer and supplier change their strategy when a crucial issue for the buyer is addressed. ### 2.3. Negotiation training

Over the past decade, organizations around the world have invested billions in negotiation training to enhance the skills of their personnel, aiming to improve negotiation outcomes, processes, and relationships ( [Movius, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib55); [Zerres et al., 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib102)). Various commercial instructional tools have been developed for this purpose, including lectures, PowerPoint presentations, [case studies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/case-study), theoretical readings, simulations with role instructions, self-assessment tools, videos, and role-play simulations ( [Tyler and Cukier, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib92)). University-based negotiation programs across various fields also employ methods like lectures, case analysis, practice and theory-based readings, discussions, reflections, internships, video analysis, [analogical reasoning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/analogical-reasoning) exercises, and [observational learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/observational-learning) ( [Fortgang, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib28); [Nadler et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib58)). However, as highlighted by other researchers, most existing training and educational programs focus primarily on tactical knowledge of integrative and distributive behaviors ( [Lewicki, 2014](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib45)) and often overlook the teaching of adaptability skills, crucial for effective negotiation ( [Putnam and Powers, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib67)). There is ample explanation of integrative and distributive strategies in educational textbooks that educators use to train students (for example, [Lax and Sebenius, 1986](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib44); [Fisher et al., 1991](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib26); [Lewicki et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib47); [Thompson, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib90)). However, there are limited guidelines available on training strategic adaptability as this topic is still relatively underexplored in academic literature ( [Putnam and Powers, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib67); [Chapman et al., 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib16); [Preuss and van der Wijst, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65); [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). Training and educational programs are called for to enhance the ability of individuals to identify negotiation patterns, interrupt unproductive interactions, and steer negotiations toward more constructive outcomes ( [Roloff et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib72)).

Below, we develop a training program that combines insights from educational science, integrating theoretical knowledge on skill development with principles of effective learning ( [Stulberg, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib83); [Barnett and Koslowski, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib6); [Macfarlane and Mayer, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib50); [McAdoo and Manwaring, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib54)).

## 3\. Theoretical foundations and outline of the strategic adaptability negotiation training

We selected Bloom's (revised) taxonomy on [learning experience](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/learning-experience) as the instructional design approach for the training activities ( [Bloom, 1956](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib8)). The taxonomy consists of six levels of cognition, including remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating ( [Krathwohl, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib41)). Given the complex and dynamic nature of negotiations, we rely on a combination of learning theories, including [constructivism](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/constructivism), situated learning theory, [social learning theory](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/social-learning-theory), and [experiential learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/experiential-learning) theory.

The core principle of _[constructivism](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/constructivism "Learn more about constructivism from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ (see e.g., [Piaget, 1950](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib63); [Bruner, 1961](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib12); [Vygotsky and Cole, 1978](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib94); [Bransford et al., 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib11)) is that successful acquisition of complex knowledge and skills requires active experimentation, and social interaction, rather than solely relying on passive forms of instruction, such as direct instruction (e.g., reading a handbook or attending a lecture). _Social and observational learning theory_ ( [Bandura, 2001](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib5)) posits that learning is a social endeavor. People learn with and from each other in social contexts. They do so by carrying out the learning or training activities together (e.g., performing tasks or missions in teams), by interacting with each other, by giving feedback or reflecting together, but also by observing each other when performing a task. _Situated learning theory_ ( [Lave and Wenger, 1991](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib43)) suggests that learning and training activities are more effective when they occur in authentic contexts, such as situations where the trained knowledge and skills need to be applied in the future. The authentic context might be a real-life situation (e.g., training on the job), but it can also be a simulated or virtual environment, a role-play, or similar. _Experiential learning theory_ ( [Kolb and Kolb, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib40)) suggests that experience and reflection on experience are powerful components of learning. Effective experiential learning involves concrete learning, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation. Based on these learning theories, we describe the accompanying learning techniques below.

_Didactic or principle-based learning_ is an educational approach focused on the explicit teaching of concepts, principles, and information. This method is characterized by a structured and often teacher-centered approach, where the instructor imparts knowledge directly to students. For example, this approach involves teaching students how they can use integrative and distributive strategies for value creation or claiming. However, this method has limitations, especially for beginners. [Novick (1988)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib59) notes that novices often struggle to apply these principles to new situations. Further research supports this observation, suggesting that providing learners with principles alone may not be as effective as other learning methods ( [Loewenstein et al., 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib49); [Nadler et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib58)). To overcome these limitations, in line with _constructivism theory,_ we integrate interactive methods in our training.

_Observational learning_ methods, consistent with _social and observational learning theory,_ consist of observing and modeling another individual to teach new behaviors or skills. This method hinges on four [cognitive processes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/cognitive-process) of attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation ( [Bandura, 1973](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib4)). Observational learning facilitates active [information processing](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/information-processing), where learners analyze and internalize observed behaviors rather than merely imitating them. This approach enhances attention and retention, critical for applying learned strategies, and leads to [tacit knowledge](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/tacit-knowledge) acquisition, allowing learners to comprehend subtle negotiation behaviors intuitively. Moreover, it enables learners to replicate behaviors observed in the model ( [Bandura, 1973](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib4)). This learning method operates without explicit strategic instruction, as learners gain insights from watching skilled negotiators guided by social feedback mechanisms inherent in [social learning theory](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/social-learning-theory) ( [Nadler et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib58)). Negotiation research particularly indicates the positive effects of observational learning through the acquired tacit knowledge ( [Polanyi, 1959](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib64)) on improving negotiation outcomes for both parties compared to learning through experience alone ( [Nadler et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib58)). Observational learning methods allow for creating realistic problems and using approaches like teacher-guided reflective inquiry. The objective of such exercises is to develop an understanding of when and how to adaptively apply an approach in a given situation rather than just focusing on executing a procedure correctly ( [Kua et al., 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib42)). When using this method, the instructor's role is to offer experience-based guidance rather than act as a sole authority on the subject ( [Clarke et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib17)).

_Implementation-intention exercises_, also in line with _social and observational learning theory_, are an effective reflective method used to cultivate behavioral skills. These exercises involve creating specific 'if-then' plans where students outline an intended action (the 'then') in response to a given situation (the 'if'). They can take the form: “If I encounter situation X, then I will perform behavior Y!” ( [Kirk et al., 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib39), p. 150). This method is particularly powerful for behavior regulation as it encourages individuals to substitute automatic behaviors with learned, alternative responses ( [Duckworth et al., 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib23)). Forming implementation intentions in negotiations facilitates pursuing prosocial goals while facing adversity ( [Trötschel and Gollwitzer, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib91)). The effectiveness of these implementation-intentions hinges largely on repetition, reinforcing the newly learned behavior ( [Gollwitzer, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib32)).

_Simulation exercises,_ consistent with _situated learning theory_ and _experiential learning theory,_ aid experiential learning ( [Movius, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib55)) and are widely used in professional schools and corporate learning environments. In negotiation education, a simulation is a structured exercise replicating real-life negotiation scenarios to help participants develop and refine their negotiating skills. Participants are assigned roles and negotiate with others to achieve specific objectives, allowing them to apply theoretical concepts, experiment with various negotiation strategies, and understand the consequences of their decisions in a controlled environment ( [Druckman and Ebner, 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib21)). By modeling complex realities, simulations place learners in specific roles and scenarios, challenging them to navigate and respond to diverse situations, typically through face-to-face communication. These scenarios might be derived from real-life or be entirely hypothetical. They allow experimentation and learning from mistakes, fostering a hands-on approach to understanding negotiation dynamics ( [Susskind and Corburn, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib84)). A common way of providing feedback after simulation exercises is by using debriefings. According to [Gardner (2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib30), debriefing provides opportunities for exploring and making sense of what happened during an event or experience, discussing what went well, and identifying what could be done to change, improve, and do differently or better next time. ## Abstract

Strategic adaptability -a key competency in Purchasing and Supply Management- is the ability to switch between integrative and distributive negotiation strategies when needed. Although its importance has been widely recognized, there remains a notable absence of dedicated training specifically designed to educate Purchasing and Supply Management students and professionals in recognizing and applying strategic adaptability during negotiations. This paper introduces a training program to fill this gap. At its core, the training utilizes a blend of educational learning methods, including [observational learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/observational-learning). It features short video clips of condensed negotiation scenarios, which provide practical insights into strategy adjustments and their effects. Feedback from students supports the engagement and efficacy of this multi-method training approach. Aiding its practical implementation, all materials are freely accessible and can be found in the [Supplementary materials](https://doi.org/10.17026/SS/OVS5DE).
