{"markdown":"## 4\. Design and development of the strategic adaptability negotiation training This section introduces our strategic adaptability negotiation training. The learning objectives are to enhance students' understanding and application of negotiation strategies, to recognize the strategies used by others, and to adapt between them. The training is easily integrated into a variety of educational settings, such as an introductory negotiation course for a large cohort of undergraduate students, as well as into a specialized negotiation course for a smaller group of students, such as in honors programs or executive education. The strategic adaptability training consists of four blocks and enhances learning through a blend of educational learning methods. This modular design allows for variations and tailoring of the training (e.g., by omitting or shortening specific blocks that do not align with the curriculum's learning objectives). For example, the training can be conducted in 135 min, divided into three 45-min sessions, or condensed into a 90-min course by excluding a block. The training fits best to students who have learned how to prepare for negotiations and the related concepts such as the best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA), zone of possible agreements (ZOPA), and reservation value (RV), which is covered in other texts and resources (e.g., [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77); [Shell, 2006](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib76); [Malhotra and Bazerman, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib52); [Thompson, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib90); [Handfield et al., 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib33)). Block 1 builds on didactic or principle-based learning, where students first develop a theoretical understanding of negotiation strategies on when and how specific strategies can be applied ( [McAdoo and Manwaring, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib54)). This is followed by three blocks with interactive elements focusing on observational learning, implementation-intention exercises, and negotiation simulations, respectively. These blocks enhance learning transfer through behavioral skill development ( [Stulberg, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib83); [Barnett and Koslowski, 2002](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib6); [Macfarlane and Mayer, 2005](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib50)). [Fig. 1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#fig1) shows the training outline and how each block targets different [cognitive processes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/cognitive-process) based on Bloom's revised taxonomy. As noted, we designed these blocks to be flexible, allowing educators to tailor the use and sequence of these methods to fit their course objectives and meet the needs of their students ( [McAdoo and Manwaring, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib54)). However, for comprehensive learning outcomes, we recommend employing all four blocks. All teaching materials are readily available. This includes lecture slides, video clips, questions to guide class discussions, and detailed video and debriefing instructions. Additionally, the implementation-intention exercise, as well as the simulation and its debriefing guidelines, are shared. The resources ensure that educators have everything to facilitate an interactive [learning experience](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/learning-experience). Please download them from this link: [Supplementary Materials](https://doi.org/10.17026/SS/OVS5DE) [1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#fn1) - 1. Block 1 has the objective of enhancing students' understanding of negotiation strategies and adaptation theories using a 30-min lecture format. The provided PowerPoint slides are purposely minimalistic and designed to allow for modifications. While explaining the negotiation concepts, the lecturer provides concrete examples of how integrative and distributive communication patterns can be recognized and applied during negotiations. For instance, an example of distributive behavior is asking for information about or discussing position, facts, or bottom line one issue at a time ( [Weingart et al., 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib97)) \- “I appreciate your perspective, but this does not work for me. Can you lower the price to meet my terms?” in contrast, an example of integrative behavior is asking for or sharing information about interests and priorities across all issues honestly ( [Weingart et al., 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib97)) \- “What concerns do you have about the property?” - 2. Block 2 relies on four video clips developed for the purpose of this training. The video clips show different environments, such as a buyer-supplier contract negotiation and a layoff negotiation, which facilitates transferability. These videos aim to reinforce the student's ability to remember and analyze communication patterns of integrative and distributive strategies and, specifically, strategic adaptations. The videos include cues for adapting strategies, as represented in [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#tbl2). These cues occur on the content, opponent, process, and context level. Over the course of approximately 45 min, students watch these video clips and engage in [group discussions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/group-discussion) guided by the lecturer. During this block, students learn the theoretical principles through practical examples, and the discussion further deepens their knowledge. An introduction video (1:30-min) is provided, which can alternatively be given by the lecturer. A more detailed overview of the video clips is provided in [Table 3](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#tbl3). ![Fig. 1](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409224000773-gr1.jpg) 1. [Download: Download high-res image (535KB)](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409224000773-gr1_lrg.jpg "Download high-res image (535KB)") 2. [Download: Download full-size image](https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409224000773-gr1.jpg "Download full-size image") Fig. 1. Outline of the learning methods used in the strategic adaptability training. The in-class discussions following the videos aim to engage students, provoke debate, and encourage reflection. The questions that guide the discussion include: “What strategy (integrative vs. distributive) and communication patterns did you observe?”; “What types of strategic adaptation did you observe?”; “Did you notice a moment where a negotiator did not respond to a cue that would warrant strategic adaptability?”; “What could alternative responses look like?”. The lecturer's role is to guide these discussions, provide experience-based insights, and encourage discussion rather than immediately offering answers. We provide instructions for the lecturer, such as video clips, questions to guide class discussion, and video and debriefing instructions. Each video has a script attached, including the ‘correct’ answers and explanations of the demonstrated strategies. - 3 Block 3 complements the previous blocks with an implementation-intention exercise. This exercise is not only a practical application of the discussed strategic adaptability concepts but also important in strengthening the students' ability to actively recall and apply these concepts in different negotiation scenarios. With this exercise, students are encouraged to replace their instinctive behaviors with newly learned responses. We achieve this by providing students with "if-then statement" outlines for each of the four strategic adaptation categories as detailed in [Table 2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#tbl2). An example statement for the process category is “ _If I encounter a moment ripe for a strategic adaptation on the process level which could occur due to … in my next negotiation, then …_”. To enhance the learning impact, students are instructed to mentally rehearse these statements three times, a method suggested by [Gollwitzer et al. (2017)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib31) to aid in internalizing responses. This exercise takes approximately 15 min. - 4 Block 4 consists of a simulation exercise where students can experiment with various negotiation strategies, allowing them to apply what they have learned in a new setting. This exercise, including preparation, negotiation, and debriefing, can be completed within 45 min. Additional time would allow for more thorough reflection and feedback. The simulation itself is a one-on-one negotiation adapted from [Heunis et al. (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35) that challenges students to use both integrative and distributive strategies. The scenario involves negotiating terms between a Dutch startup, "Green-karts," as the buyer and an Indian e-motor manufacturer, "Drive Limited," as the supplier. The negotiation covers four key issues with different priority levels: the quality and price of the e-motor, the currency for the payment, and [international commercial terms](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/incoterms) (incoterms) for transport. ## 5\. Training implementation and validation We tested the proof of concept in one large undergraduate course and two smaller extracurricular programs at the researcher's university to evaluate its effectiveness, strengths, and weaknesses. The student groups were considered separately because they are substantially different (e.g., based on the group size (large vs. small), student motivation (mandatory vs. voluntary), and study background (PSM vs. mixed). The large group of undergraduate students followed a mandatory two-day workshop in a PSM course (N = 93). Of this group, 70 students provided background information on gender (65% were male) and nationality (16 different nationalities, 56% Dutch, 31% Other-European, and 13% Non-European). The smaller groups followed nine-month extracurricular negotiation programs consisting of up to 20 selected undergraduate and graduate students from various academic backgrounds. Combined, the smaller groups consisted of 34 students (18 graduate and 16 undergraduate, of which 68% were male) with a background in a variety of study programs (17 different nationalities, 30% Dutch, 42% Other-European, and 28% Non-European) participated in our training. All student groups were relatively new to the negotiation subject and only received prior training on fundamental negotiation concepts and preparation. For the purpose of the training validation, we collected data. Students received a post-questionnaire, including questions about their satisfaction with the training. [2](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#fn2) This data collection was approved by the ethics committee of the authors’ faculty and did not pose any risks to participants. Participation in the data collection was voluntary and confidential. Satisfaction was measured on a [Likert scale](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/likert-scale) from 1 extremely dissatisfied to 10 extremely satisfied with “ _How satisfied are you with the lecture component of this training?”_ Furthermore, students were asked open questions to highlight what they found useful and what could be improved by answering “ _What did you find most useful in this lecture?_” and “ _What could be improved in this lecture?_” In total, 74 students filled out the survey in the undergraduate course and 33 in the extracurricular programs. ### 5.1. The undergraduate student group's average training satisfaction score was 7.34 (out of 10, SD = 1.68), and the extracurricular student group's score was 8.03 (SD = 1.49). We deliberately kept this part short as further details would follow in _Block 2_. We noticed that at this stage, students seemed to have only a vague understanding of the strategic adaptability cues and, at the same time, did not raise many questions. In _Block 2_, the video examples clearly enhanced students' ability to recognize and understand adaptations, sparking lively discussions. During the discussion, students reflected on the challenges of monitoring strategies during the negotiation process, as well as the benefits of mastering both strategies. Overall, students showed an increased awareness and understanding of strategic adaptability, which is important to become a more adaptable negotiator. Reflecting on the students’ evaluations showed that they especially appreciated the practical application through the videos and the interactive learning environment. Students in the extracurricular group indicated that. - - _“It made switching between strategies and reasons to do so more conscious. Having the 4 reasons on the front of the mind substantiates a strategy shift by giving it clear reasons while keeping one aware of stimulus that could lead to opponent shifts.”_ - - _“It gives a different perspective from just negotiating yourself as you focus more on the effect a certain behavior has on others while usually, you're thinking about your plan instead.”_ - - _“Discussing the situation in the video and_ _[hearing](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/sensation-of-hearing "Learn more about hearing from ScienceDirect's AI-generated Topic Pages")_ _how others felt about certain behaviors was very helpful as they might view it differently than me.”_ The undergraduate student group mentioned that. - - _“The portrayal helps understand negotiations as a strategic and dynamic back-and-forth instead of it being static and determined before it starts.”_ - - _“To see different case examples. You can see what might happen, put yourself into the situation, consider what you would do, and have to pay attention to.”_ - - _“The in-class discussion, including everyone giving their opinions and views on the videos.”_ - - _“To get information that we could practically apply.”_ Furthermore, the extracurricular student groups valued the enhanced theoretical understanding and strategy awareness gained through the training. They appreciated learning how strategies affect the negotiation, when to switch a strategy, and gaining awareness of one's own and others' negotiation styles. For example, students mentioned. - - _“It was useful to learn about the adaptability of oneself, how to evaluate the situation and act accordingly to the strategy needed to reach a goal. I also liked the awareness of identifying possible issues and how to respond to them. Great session!”_ - - _“The realization that a mixture of both styles can be applied in the same negotiation was quite helpful.”_ - - _“I found the tips on how to sense cues on when to change strategy, as well as ways to categorize them to be most useful.”_ Even though the training has shown to be effective, there are points of improvement that can be considered for future implementations. First, the extracurricular student group highly appreciated the enhanced theoretical understanding and awareness of strategies, while the undergraduate student group thought the training was a bit lengthy. This was indicated by students reporting under points of improvement, for instance, _“The length of the negotiation training.”_ Hence, for a larger group of more junior students, the theoretical discussion should only include the basics, which can be further elaborated on during the video discussions. For the extracurricular student group, which seems to be more dedicated, theory is appreciated. Second, both student groups would like to discuss more examples or have in-class demonstrations. To provide an example quote for each group, a student from the undergraduate student group suggested, _“There could be more time to study the 4 adaptations and discuss more examples.”_ A student from the extracurricular student group proposed that _“The audience could be asked to come up with specific examples of each style to discuss the subtle differences between them.”_ Therefore, the instructor could, for example, encourage a lengthier discussion on students' examples when performing the implementation intention exercise. Alternatively, the one-on-one negotiation simulation could be replaced with a fishbowl negotiation (see [Bordone and Carr (2013)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib9) for a more detailed explanation). Here, a selected group of students is asked to negotiate in front of the class. The instructor interrupts or pauses the negotiation to analyze specific moments (e.g., strategic shifts) with the class. Such a setting provides further examples and active engagement for students. ## 6\. Discussion Even though negotiation is an important skill in the PSM domain ( [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3); [Stek and Schiele, 2021](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib82); [Kelly and Chicksand, 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib37)), there is a lack of understanding among professionals regarding negotiation strategies ( [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77); [Ramsay, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68)). This specifically concerns strategic adaptability, the competence of applying both integrative and distributive negotiation strategies, and switching between them when needed. Strategic adaptability allows negotiators to anticipate and monitor the other's actions as well as other cues (e.g., new content information) in order to adjust their strategies accordingly ( [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). To train the competency of strategic adaptability we developed a training program, combining the learning theories of [constructivism](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/constructivism), situated learning theory, [social learning theory](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/social-learning-theory), and [experiential learning](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/economics-econometrics-and-finance/experiential-learning) theory. Central to our training are observational learning methods building on four videos of a negotiation situation showing students a variety of negotiation adaptations and their effects. We showcase to negotiation lecturers and trainers both the design process of our strategic adaptability training as well as the results from the first iteration, focusing on its implementation and evaluation. With the training, we make two contributions to the PSM and broader negotiation literature. First, while integrative and distributive strategies have been addressed in the PSM literature before (e.g., see [Ramsay, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib68); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib101)), prior studies did not explore how to apply and adapt between these strategies. Some even treated them as mutually exclusive ( [Munduate et al., 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib56); [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib101)). Despite the recognition of adaptability in negotiation literature, such as turning points (e.g., see [Druckman, 2001](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib20); [Olekalns and Weingart, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib62); [Druckman and Olekalns, 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib22)) and phase models (e.g., see [Olekalns et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib60); [Weingart and Olekalns, 2004](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib99)), there has been a call for training in strategic adaptability ( [Roloff et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib72); [Putnam and Powers, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib67); [Chapman et al., 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib16); [Preuss and van der Wijst, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65); [Heunis et al., 2024](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib35)). To our knowledge, this training is the first systematic attempt to prepare students on dynamic negotiation processes and explicitly on adapting between integrative and distributive strategies. Second, although our focus is specifically on negotiation strategies, our training relates to PSM strategies more generally. Integrative and distributive strategies link to concepts such as pie expansion, power and trust in B2B negotiations, buyer-supplier satisfaction, and preparation in sourcing processes ( [Spekman, 1988](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib79); [Jap, 1999](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib36); [Smeltzer et al., 2003](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77); [Zachariassen, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib101); [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73); [Ried et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib71)). Hence, learning about adaptability not only enhances negotiation strategies but also relates to concepts in the PSM literature more general. For example, buyers and suppliers negotiate to align supply with demand, a process critical for organizational competitiveness ( [Tassabehji and Moorhouse, 2008](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib85); [Åge and Eklinder-Frick, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib1); [Bals et al., 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib3)). To do this effectively, negotiators need to understand the impact of their strategies on buyer-supplier relationships. While integrative strategies are often favored for their satisfaction outcomes ( [Fleming and Hawes, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib27)), both integrative and distributive tactics can be employed within the same negotiation ( [Preuss and van der Wijst, 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib65); [Saorín-Iborra and Cubillo, 2019](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib73)). Key questions surrounding power and trust relate to whether a buying firm should pressure or pamper its suppliers (e.g., [Pulles et al., 2014](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib66)). These concepts relate to integrative and distributive strategies and our training enhances purchasers' awareness of their potential strategic consequences, increasing skills at navigating complex relationships. ## 7\. Limitations & future research While our training was well-received by students, we have not yet tested it with executives and purchasing professionals. As a result, we cannot confirm its effectiveness for these professional groups. Regardless, as indicated by the study of [Smeltzer et al. (2003)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib77), many professionals still lack an understanding of integrative and distributive negotiation strategies. Based on this indication, we expect our training program to be beneficial for training among professionals, for example, in executive training. Our teaching experience suggests that practitioners in these trainings are highly motivated to improve their skills. Therefore, we advise following the recommendations of the extracurricular training groups for professional programs. Another limitation is the complexity of the negotiation task used in the training. While complex negotiations (multiple issues to agree on) offer greater flexibility and trade-off opportunities for coming to an agreement, they also increase the information load with regard to the content of the simulation, potentially hindering participants' ability to explore and utilize these opportunities effectively ( [Warsitzka et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib96)). Usually, a simulation provides greater learning effects when students have gained experience with a simpler simulation (fewer issues to agree on) beforehand. To ensure the effectiveness of the training and optimize learning, the complexity of the negotiation simulation should be based on the students’ prior negotiation experience with simulations. Should the curriculum permit, we recommend increasing the simulation complexity over time ( [Susskind and Corburn, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib84)), starting with a simpler, single-issue simulation. For future research, we recommend exploring the long-term effects and the effectiveness of training using similar design processes and combinations of learning methods, and examining to what extent training refreshers could contribute to it. [Baber (2022)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib2) examined the long-term impacts of negotiation training on negotiators and organizations, confirming that trained negotiators influence organizations by leading negotiations and achieving success. However, there is limited information on the duration of training required for students to become considerably better negotiators. Measuring effectiveness could involve comparing the negotiation results of groups with and without the training over an extended period and monitoring students' behavioral improvements. Instructors or coaches might also consider integrating training refreshers to boost the effectiveness and mitigate retention decline ( [Soderstrom and Bjork, 2015](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib78)), potentially taking the form of reflections and mentoring ( [Fortgang, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib28); [Chapman et al., 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib16)). Moreover, future research could also focus on reflective practices and their role in helping students learn complex skills. Reflection involves continuously evaluating one's learning practices to gain a deeper understanding and improvement ( [Schön, 1983](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib75)). For instance, students can enhance their strategic adaptability by reflecting on their negotiation performance and turning experiences into learning ( [Boud et al., 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib10)). Reflective practices have been demonstrated to be effective in debriefing negotiation simulations ( [Susskind and Corburn, 2000](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib84); [McAdoo and Manwaring, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib54); [Druckman and Ebner, 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib21)). Additionally, video playback is a useful debriefing tool, allowing participants to see their actual performance, which helps reduce hindsight bias ( [Fanning and Gaba, 2007](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1478409224000773#bib25)). Although the benefits of video playback in debriefing have been reported, further exploration into its consistency and effectiveness is needed. Overall, the ambition of our training program is to invite and inspire PSM lecturers and trainers to teach their students about the importance of strategic adaptability. We believe our training design can be applied to various topics in PSM education. We envision that the open-access teaching materials, grounded in evidence-based educational learning methods derived from various learning theories, offer a solid, engaging, and easy-to-implement addition to more traditional learning approaches.","metadata":{"dc.identifier":"10.1016/j.pursup.2024.100968","SDTech":"Proudly brought to you by the SD Technology team","citation_title":"Strategic adaptability negotiation training in purchasing and supply management: A multi-method instructional approach","citation_publication_date":"2025/03/01","ogDescription":"Strategic adaptability -a key competency in Purchasing and Supply Management- is the ability to switch between integrative and distributive negotiatio…","tdm-reservation":"1","citation_type":"JOUR","ogTitle":"Strategic adaptability negotiation training in purchasing and supply management: A multi-method instructional approach","tdm-policy":"https://www.elsevier.com/tdm/tdmrep-policy.json","viewport":"initial-scale=1","robots":"INDEX,FOLLOW,NOARCHIVE,NOCACHE,NOODP,NOYDIR","citation_fulltext_world_readable":"","og:image":"https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409225X00030-cov200h.gif","citation_article_type":"Full-length article","og:type":"article","citation_firstpage":"100968","citation_issue":"2","citation_volume":"31","ogImage":"https://ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/1-s2.0-S1478409225X00030-cov200h.gif","title":"Strategic adaptability negotiation training in purchasing and supply management: A multi-method instructional approach - 1	{"markdown":"# A Critical Exploration of Bargaining in Purchasing and Supply Management: A Systematic Literature Review

## Abstract

Bargaining with suppliers is a key Purchasing and Supply Management (PSM) activity but there is considerable ambiguity over what bargaining entails and the concept currently lacks a systematic treatment, despite its significant interest to PSM professionals. The literature shows that bargaining can be seen as an adversarial approach to negotiation (in contrast to more integrative/collaborative ones) and also the back-and-forth discussion over price and other variables between buying and supplying organisations to reach an agreement. In addition, many will move between fundamentally distributive and integrative approaches as the discussions play out. A systematic literature review of the Scopus, ProQuest, ScienceDirect, JSTOR and Web of Science databases was undertaken to address this gap, identifying 427 relevant journal papers that were systematically analysed. First, descriptive techniques identified the trajectory of published papers, methods, theories and their industrial context. Second, content analysis identified the key constructs and associated operational measures/variables of bargaining. Third, the constructs have then been ordered temporally and by areas of location (organisational/departmental and individual levels) to generate a model and inform a series of practice-based recommendations at different stages of the bargaining process. The findings will allow future researchers to use the constructs either directly in developing focused hypotheses to test relationships or as a basis for refinement and extension in cumulative theory building and testing. In addition, a series of focused research gaps have been identified, such as addressing the current contradictory findings of the effect of purchasing volume or organisational size on bargaining power.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Negotiation

Negotiation is the interpersonal back-and-forth communication that allows two (or more) parties to come to an agreed-upon joint decision when they have oppositional (and sometimes shared) preferences and interests (Fisher et al. [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR61 "Fisher R, Ury W, Patton B (1991) Getting to yes: negotiating an agreement without giving in (2nd ed) Sydney: century business. Asia Pac J Hum Resour 34:125–126"); Bazerman and Moore [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR19 "Bazerman M, Moore D (2008) Judgment in managerial decision making, 7th edn. New York, Wiley")). It is an ubiquitous part of life and individuals engage in these processes regularly in both their private and professional lives (Vetschera [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR183 "Vetschera R (2013) Negotiation processes: an integrated perspective. EURO J Decis Process 1:135–164")).

In a commercial context, Business-to-business (B2B) negotiation is an integral part of business activities (Li et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR112 "Li H, Huang C, Su S, Higdon B (2002) Design and implementation of business objects for automated business negotiations. Group Decis Negot 11(1):23–44")) and can be seen as: “…the application of general negotiation principles to business settings, such as buying tangible or intangible goods, or acquiring services” (Li et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR112 "Li H, Huang C, Su S, Higdon B (2002) Design and implementation of business objects for automated business negotiations. Group Decis Negot 11(1):23–44"): 24) and is a critically important element in the exchange of goods and services between organisations (Anderson and Narus [1990](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR9 "Anderson J, Narus J (1990) A model of distributor firm and manufacturer firm working partnerships. J Mark 54(1):42–58")). The decisions and choices taken in the negotiation process affect organisational outcomes and potentially their overall profitability (Balakrishnan and Eliashberg [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR14 "Balakrishnan P, Eliashberg J (1995) An analytical process model of two-party negotiations. Manage Sc 41(2):226–243")) through the inter-organisational exchange of resources, such as goods, services, skills and information (Barnum and Wolniansky [1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR16 "Barnum C, Wolniansky N (1989) Taking cues from body language. Manag Rev 78(6):59–60")). In the Purchasing and Supply (PSM) context, individuals, acting as representatives of buying and selling organisations, negotiate to match supply and demand factors and these are often complicated by the need to reflect a range of stakeholders in a single negotiation (Eklinder-Frick and Åge [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR54 "Eklinder-Frick J, Åge LJ (2017) Goal oriented balancing: happy-happy negotiations beyond win-win situations. J Bus Ind Mark 32(4):525–534"); Lempereur and Pekar [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR107 "Lempereur A, Pekar M (2017) The distributive knot: negotiators’ responsibility to untie complex demand. J Bus Ind Mark 32:535–540")). Negotiation skills and competencies are regularly identified as being important and seen as a key driver of organisational competitiveness (Tassabehji and Moorhouse [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR173 "Tassabehji R, Moorhouse A (2008) The changing role of procurement: developing professional effectiveness. J Purch Supply Manag 14(1):55–68"); Bals et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR15 "Bals L, Schulze H, Kelly S, Stek K (2019) Purchasing and supply management (PSM) competencies: Current and future requirements. J Purch Supply Manag 25(5):100572")), in particular, as being a key cost-saving lever (Úbeda et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR179 "Úbeda R, Alsua C, Carrasco N (2015) Purchasing models and organizational performance: a study of key strategic tools. J Bus Res 68(2):177–188")).

### 1.2 Strategies and Approaches

Both research and practice have tended to perceive negotiation as being largely based on two broad strategies (Walton and McKersie [1965a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR184 "Walton RE, McKersie RB (1965a) A behavioral theory of labor negotiations. McGraw-Hill"), [b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR186 "Walton R, McKersie R (1965b) A behavioral theory of labor relations. McGraw-Hill, New York")). First, a distributive strategy that refers to the behaviour negotiators adopt when they try to claim as much value as they can for themselves, which leads to fundamentally win-lose outcomes. It is often this type of negotiation, i.e., “adversarial bargaining \[that\] most people think of when they think of negotiating: haggling over price, getting to the bottom line when one dollar more for you is one less for me” (Buckley [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR29 "Buckley R (2001) Adversarial bargaining: an ignored aspect of negotiation theory. Aust Law J 75:181–189"): 181).

Second, an integrative strategy, where more collaborative behaviours are focused on creating joint value leading to win–win outcomes and: “…in bargaining co-operatively, negotiators seek common ground…they communicate a sense of shared interests and values and use reason and logic to seek co-operation. Their goal is to reach a fair and just agreement” (Buckley [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR29 "Buckley R (2001) Adversarial bargaining: an ignored aspect of negotiation theory. Aust Law J 75:181–189"): 181). Developing these broad strategies, Fisher et al. ( [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR61 "Fisher R, Ury W, Patton B (1991) Getting to yes: negotiating an agreement without giving in (2nd ed) Sydney: century business. Asia Pac J Hum Resour 34:125–126")) popularised a distinction between interest-based (principled) negotiation, being a more structured integrative approach that relies on identifying the interests of the other party and then generating options to reach a mutually acceptable agreement, and then competitive bargaining, which is essentially the same as adversarial bargaining (Buckley [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR29 "Buckley R (2001) Adversarial bargaining: an ignored aspect of negotiation theory. Aust Law J 75:181–189")). In B2B negotiations, it is often perceived that negotiators are more satisfied with an integrative strategy (Fleming and Hawes [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR62 "Fleming D, Hawes J (2017) The negotiation scorecard: a planning tool in business and industrial marketing. J Bus Ind Mark 32(4):519–524")), but it has also been noted that both integrative and distributive tactics may be deployed in the same bargaining situation (Preuss and van der Wijst [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR147 "Preuss M, Wijst P (2017) A phase-specific analysis of negotiation styles. J Bus Ind Mark 32(10):1")).

### 1.3 Process Perspective

In common with other PSM activities, negotiation has been distilled into a series of process-based steps (see Vetschera [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR183 "Vetschera R (2013) Negotiation processes: an integrated perspective. EURO J Decis Process 1:135–164") for a useful summary). These range from relatively simple models showing steps in which a negotiator makes an initial offer and establishing rules when it is ‘best’ for the other party to accept this offer, what counteroffers should be made and when to quit the negotiation (Lopes and Coelho [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR120 "Lopes F, Coelho H (2010) Concession Behaviour in Automated Negotiation. In: Buccafurri F, Semeraro G (eds) E-Commerce and Web Technologies. EC-Web 2010. Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing, vol 61. Springer, Berlin")). Others are more activity-focused, in which: “…at least three steps are traditionally identified…including planning or preparation; negotiation, bargaining or interaction; and striking a deal” (Agndal et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR3 "Agndal H, Åge LJ, Eklinder-Frick JO (2017) Review of Two decades of business negotiation research: an overview and suggestions for future studies. J Bus Ind Mark 32(4):487–504"): 493) and other more complex ones, such as Adair and Brett’s ( [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR2 "Adair W, Brett J (2005) The negotiation dance: time, culture, and behavioral sequences in negotiation. Organ Sci 16(1):33–52")) negotiation dance, that encompasses time, culture, and behavioural sequences.

Seeing bargaining as a set of specific activities within a wider negotiation process, we can identify early modelling work that generated two major process approaches (Tutzauer [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR178 "Tutzauer F (1992) The communication of offers in dyadic bargaining. In: Putnam L, Roloff ME (eds) Communication and negotiation. Sage, Newbury Park, pp 67–82")) to explore bargaining. First, those that are static in nature and use only general characteristics, and second, those developed in the 1950s and 1960s using Game Theory that shows the process as being one of an offer-by-offer basis (Harsanyi [1956](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR77 "Harsanyi J (1956) Approaches to the bargaining problem before and after the theory of games: a critical discussion of Zeuthen’s, Hicks’, and Nash’s theories. Econometrica 24(2):1"); Bishop [1964](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR25 "Bishop R (1964) A Zeuthen-Hicks theory of bargaining. Econometrica XXXII 3:410–417")). These models can be simple in nature, in which the discussion, exchange and agreement on bargaining issues, focus on single-issue variables and concessions. Of note is the Nash equilibrium, which: “…is a set of strategies, one for each of the n players of a game, that has the property that each player's choice is his best response to the choices of the n–1 other players” (Holt and Roth [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR86 "Holt C, Roth A (2004) The Nash equilibrium: a perspective. PNAS 101(12):3999–4002"): 3999). Examples are Raiffa’s model ( [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR149 "Raiffa H (1982) The art and science of negotiation. Harvard University Press, Boston")), in which the decisions of one party are based on the other’s proposal which may also lead to a change in the offer(s) being made.

Multi-variable/issue situations become considerably more complex, as negotiators may take multidimensional positions by changing how demanding they are across a range of concessions. Later models have explicitly considered these types of negotiations. John and Raith ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR92 "John R, Raith M (2001) Optimizing multi-stage negotiations. J Econ Behav Organ 45(2):155–173")) factor in the possibility of these different issues and Tajima and Fraser ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR172 "Tajima M, Fraser N (2001) Logrolling procedure for multi-issue negotiation. Group Decis Negot 10:217–235")) develop a log-rolling approach where two parties mutually determine how to improve both their negotiation positions. Similar approaches can be seen in work such as Ehtamo et al. ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR53 "Ehtamo H, Kettunen E, Hämäläinen R (2001) Searching for joint gains in multi-party negotiations. Eur J Oper Res 130:54–69")) which factors in situations where the negotiator’s preferences are affected by incomplete information. Despite these models developing the perspective of multi-issue bargaining, they are still somewhat restrictive, i.e., John and Raith ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR92 "John R, Raith M (2001) Optimizing multi-stage negotiations. J Econ Behav Organ 45(2):155–173")) only deal with one issue at a time and Tajima and Fraser ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR172 "Tajima M, Fraser N (2001) Logrolling procedure for multi-issue negotiation. Group Decis Negot 10:217–235")) only consider one possible trade-off step.

Classical game-theoretic bargaining models do provide a useful normative perspective on achieving the optimal outcomes for a bargaining situation, but they are only really suitable in defined situations with clear parameters. As such models are not intended to be descriptive representations of actual negotiations, they consequently do not provide full instructions for negotiators to choose which courses of action will lead to the most optimal outcomes (Lau et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR104 "Lau R, Wong O, Li Y, Ma L (2008) Mining trading partners’ preferences for efficient multi-issue bargaining in e-business. J Manag Inf Syst 25(1):79–104")). Therefore, there still remains the opportunity for research to assist individuals to bargain more effectively (Raiffa [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR149 "Raiffa H (1982) The art and science of negotiation. Harvard University Press, Boston")) in how they deploy tactics, rather than focusing on (just) the variables themselves, as these may affect the later relationships that are developed with the other party (Kun-Chang and Soon-Jae [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR102 "Kun-Chang L, Soon-Jae K (2006) A causal knowledge-driven negotiation mechanism for B2B electronic commerce. Intelligent decision-making support systems: foundations, applications and challenges. Springer, London, pp 167–186"); Theron et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR174 "Theron E, Boshoff C, Terblanche N (2008) The antecedents of relationship commitment in the management of relationships in business-to-business (B2B) financial services. J Mark Manag 24(9–10):997–1010")).

### 1.4 How has Bargaining been Defined and Categorised?

There is a wide range of negotiation research in many other fields, such as labour relations and politics (see Agndal et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR3 "Agndal H, Åge LJ, Eklinder-Frick JO (2017) Review of Two decades of business negotiation research: an overview and suggestions for future studies. J Bus Ind Mark 32(4):487–504") for a useful literature review in the B2B field) and in PSM on the wider context of negotiation. However, given the importance of bargaining evident in the strategies/approaches to and the processes of negotiation, this specific aspect of negotiation has received far less academic intention and clarity on what actually happens during B2B negotiations remains scarce (Fells et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR59 "Fells R, Caspersz D, Leighton C (2018) The encouragement of bargaining in good faith—a behavioural approach. Ind Relat J 60(2):266–281"); Geiger [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR68 "Geiger I (2017) A model of negotiation issue–based tactics in business-to-business sales negotiations. Ind Mark Manag 64:91–106")). As seen in the above discussions, there is conceptual and definitional ambiguity about the bargaining concept and the terms ‘bargaining’ and ‘negotiation’ are often used interchangeably (Warntjen [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR189 "Warntjen A (2011) Bargaining. In: Encyclopedia of power, pp 55–60"); Steinel and Harinck [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR166 "Steinel W, Harinck, F (2020) Negotiation and Bargaining. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Psychology")).

What can be distilled from the extant literature, is that bargaining, as being synonymous with ‘haggling’, can be seen as a specific type and approach to negotiation in which two parties dispute an issue (often price) with the goal of coming to an end agreement. This adversarial approach is mainly contrasted with more integrative and collaborative ones as proposed by Walton and McKersie ( [1965a](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR184 "Walton RE, McKersie RB (1965a) A behavioral theory of labor negotiations. McGraw-Hill"), [b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR186 "Walton R, McKersie R (1965b) A behavioral theory of labor relations. McGraw-Hill, New York")) and Fisher et al. ( [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR61 "Fisher R, Ury W, Patton B (1991) Getting to yes: negotiating an agreement without giving in (2nd ed) Sydney: century business. Asia Pac J Hum Resour 34:125–126")). Second, bargaining may also be seen as those discussions in which parties attempt to reach an agreement over a narrower range of variables/requirements (often price) and is contrasted with those negotiations that are more complex with multiple issues (Rubin and Brown [1976](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR152 "Rubin J, Brown B (1976) The social psychology of bargaining and negotiation. Adm Sci Q 21:1")). Third, bargaining can be seen as a specific stage in the negotiation process consisting of activities such as opening and evaluating options and reflecting the back-and-forth discussions between two or more parties as they strive to reach an agreement.

Although bargaining is most closely associated with competitive/adversarial approaches and despite Fisher et al. ( [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR61 "Fisher R, Ury W, Patton B (1991) Getting to yes: negotiating an agreement without giving in (2nd ed) Sydney: century business. Asia Pac J Hum Resour 34:125–126")) assertion that principle, interest-based, cooperative approaches are the best choice, it is clear that individuals and organisations do not necessarily follow just one and may change during negotiations with suppliers. However, it is clear that some form of back and forward discussions are needed, even when they are seen as being more integrative in nature. Further, individuals and organisations may adopt both integrative and distributive approaches depending on what the negotiation situation requires. Haggling has been covered extensively in the consumer-focused literature but is seen as a ‘dark art’ of B2B negotiations and considered somewhat unsavoury, although it has been noted that: “…once the end game is reached, an adversarial strategy is usually required to achieve the best result and an attempt to avoid conflict at this point will often lead to a less than optimal result” (Buckley [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR29 "Buckley R (2001) Adversarial bargaining: an ignored aspect of negotiation theory. Aust Law J 75:181–189"): 183). We suggest that the prevalence and possibly the importance of bargaining, as the ‘haggling’ and discussion activity in the middle of the negotiation process is more prevalent in what Fisher et al. ( [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR61 "Fisher R, Ury W, Patton B (1991) Getting to yes: negotiating an agreement without giving in (2nd ed) Sydney: century business. Asia Pac J Hum Resour 34:125–126")) term competitive bargaining, there will nonetheless be similar activities sometimes deployed in principled negotiations. In addition, purchasing portfolio approaches, for example, Kraljic’s matrix, identify categories of spend that necessitate more adversarial approaches to supply management and how suppliers in these categories are negotiated with. Therefore, this research will be useful for a range of negotiation scenarios.

This paper aims to provide greater clarity through the identification of robust constructs and variables/measures that will generate a fuller understanding of what is meant by bargaining and complements the extant B2B negotiation literature. The contribution of this paper is to synthesise the extant literature by first describing its current state and then making an explicit theoretical contribution by establishing a set of constructs and measures/variables that are then developing a model which orders these temporally and where they are most often located, i.e., at the levels of the organisational/departmental, individual and a mix of the two. This will complement existing work, such as Agndal et al. ( [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR3 "Agndal H, Åge LJ, Eklinder-Frick JO (2017) Review of Two decades of business negotiation research: an overview and suggestions for future studies. J Bus Ind Mark 32(4):487–504")) which looks at the wider negotiation context, those that focus on other parts of the negotiation process, e.g. Peterson and Lucas ( [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR145 "Peterson R, Lucas G (2001) Expanding the antecedent components of the traditional business negotiation model: pre-negotiation literature review and planning-preparation propositions. J Mark Theory Pract 9(4):37–49")) which looks at the preparation phase in business negotiation and those from a seller’s perspective (e.g., Simintiras and Thomas [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR161 "Simintiras A, Thomas A (1998) Cross-cultural sales negotiations: a literature review and research propositions. Int Mark Rev 15(1):10–28")) which, whilst useful, will naturally promote ways in which selling organisations can increase their bargaining power or bargain more efficiently. Looking further ahead, the potential for increased usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the bargaining process (Gottge et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR72 "Gottge S, Menzel T, Forslund H (2020) Industry 4.0 technologies in the purchasing process. Ind Manag Data Syst 20(4):730–748")) suggests a clearer understanding of bargaining is needed to help establish parameters and rules for such systems.

This rationale has been used to establish three focused research questions and follows the approach of Ali et al. ( [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR6 "Ali A, Mahfouz A, Arisha A (2017) Analysing supply chain resilience: integrating the constructs in a concept mapping framework via a systematic literature review. Int J Supply Chain Manag 22(1):16–39")) in which a literature review was used to integrate the constructs in a concept mapping framework for supply chain resilience:

RQ1. What are the theoretical and methodological trends in PSM bargaining research?

RQ2. What are the constructs and measures/variables used to define bargaining?

RQ3. How do the bargaining constructs interrelate to improve conceptual clarity and generate practice recommendations?

The paper is structured as follows. First, the methodology sets out the parameters of the systematic literature review and the process of identification and analysis are explained. Second, the findings and discussion section is divided into two parts. The first adopts a descriptive approach to address RQ1 by identifying how the extant literature has theoretically and methodologically approached the field and the industrial contexts in which the research has been conducted. Then an analytical approach to the development of the constructs and measures/variables (RQ2) and their amalgamation into a temporally and location-orientated model (RQ3). Finally, the gaps identified are distilled into relevant and focused areas for future research and the limitations of this research are highlighted.

## 2 Methodology

The methodology of this paper follows the often-used approach of Denyer and Tranfield ( [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR47 "Denyer D, Tranfield D (2009) Producing a systematic review. In: Buchanan DA, Bryman A (eds) The Sage handbook of organizational research methods. Sage Publications Ltd., New York, pp 671–689")) and one that is used in similar systematic literature reviews in the field (e.g., Ali et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR6 "Ali A, Mahfouz A, Arisha A (2017) Analysing supply chain resilience: integrating the constructs in a concept mapping framework via a systematic literature review. Int J Supply Chain Manag 22(1):16–39"); Chicksand et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR39 "Chicksand D, Watson G, Walker H, Radnor Z, Johnston R (2012) Theoretical perspectives in purchasing and supply chain management: An analysis of the literature. J Supply Chain Manag 17:454–472"); Walker et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#ref-CR185 "Walker H, Chicksand D, Radnor Z, Watson G (2015) Theoretical perspectives in operations management: an analysis of the literature. Int J Oper Prod Manag 35(8):1182–1206")), with the first four steps shown in this methodology section and step 5 appearing in the findings and discussion sections (Fig. [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10726-024-09879-9#Fig1)).
